subtopic_detail: COVID-19 severity assessment and dexamethasone indication
stem: A 72-year-old man presents with 5 days of cough, fever, and progressive dyspnoea. He has type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease stage 3b. A SARS-CoV-2 rapid antigen test is positive. He is commenced on supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs at 4 L/min to maintain saturation above 92%.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 98 bpm, BP 136/78 mmHg, RR 24/min, SpO2 89% on room air (94% on 4 L NP), T 38.4 C
data_table.Investigations: WCC 8.2 x10^9/L, CRP 124 mg/L, lymphocytes 0.6 x10^9/L, Cr 186 micromol/L (baseline 152), chest X-ray bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological intervention at this stage?

options.text: Oral nirmatrelvir-ritonavir 300/100 mg twice daily for 5 days to reduce viral replication
IV remdesivir 200 mg loading dose then 100 mg daily as the sole additional treatment
Commence empiric IV amoxicillin with clavulanic acid for presumed bacterial co-infection based on the CRP
Oral paracetamol and supportive care only until further oxygen escalation is required
Oral dexamethasone 6 mg daily for up to 10 days alongside standard supportive care

stem: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation, stable ischaemic heart disease, and COPD presents to his GP on day 2 of mild COVID-19 symptoms confirmed by rapid antigen test. He has a persistent dry cough and mild fatigue but no dyspnoea or hypoxia. His regular medications include rivaroxaban 20 mg daily, ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, tiotropium inhaler, and salbutamol as needed.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78 bpm irregular, BP 128/76 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 96% on room air, T 37.8 C
data_table.Investigations: eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73m2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to antiviral therapy?

options.text: Switch rivaroxaban to enoxaparin, switch ticagrelor to clopidogrel, and suspend atorvastatin during the course
Withhold rivaroxaban and ticagrelor during the 5-day nirmatrelvir-ritonavir course plus 3 days after
Prescribe molnupiravir as an alternative antiviral that avoids these drug interactions entirely
Withhold ticagrelor and switch rivaroxaban to enoxaparin for the treatment course plus washout period
Commence nirmatrelvir-ritonavir at standard dose with no medication adjustments needed

subtopic_detail: Levodopa wearing-off phenomenon recognition and management
stem: A 71-year-old man with Parkinson disease diagnosed 6 years ago presents with increasing difficulty with mobility over the past 4 months. He was initially well controlled on levodopa-carbidopa 100/25 mg three times daily. He now describes predictable worsening of tremor, rigidity, and slowness in the 30 to 60 minutes before each dose is due. He is independent with activities of daily living during on-periods.

data_table.Examination: Currently in off-state: moderate resting tremor right hand, cogwheel rigidity bilateral upper limbs, shuffling gait with reduced arm swing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial adjustment to manage this complication?

options.text: Add entacapone 200 mg with each levodopa dose to prolong peripheral levodopa availability
Increase dosing frequency to four times daily with a reduced individual dose to maintain total daily levodopa
Switch entirely to a sustained-release levodopa formulation at the same total daily dose
Add pramipexole as a dopamine agonist to provide more continuous dopaminergic stimulation
Refer for deep brain stimulation assessment given the failure of current oral medication

subtopic_detail: Impulse control disorder on dopamine agonist in Parkinson disease
stem: A 63-year-old man with Parkinson disease diagnosed 3 years ago returns for routine review. His motor symptoms are well controlled on pramipexole 1 mg three times daily. His wife reports he has spent over $18,000 on online gambling in the past 2 months and has also developed compulsive online shopping. He has no prior psychiatric history and had no behavioural issues before starting pramipexole.

data_table.Medications: Pramipexole 1 mg TDS, no other medications
data_table.Examination: Mild bilateral resting tremor, minimal rigidity, normal gait

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of this complication?

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy while continuing pramipexole at the current dose
Add an SSRI for impulse control and maintain pramipexole at the current effective dose
Gradually taper pramipexole and substitute levodopa to maintain motor symptom control
Reduce pramipexole to the lowest effective motor dose and monitor gambling behaviour monthly
Switch pramipexole to ropinirole as an alternative dopamine agonist with lower impulse risk

subtopic_detail: Neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome from acute dopaminergic withdrawal
stem: A 74-year-old woman with advanced Parkinson disease on levodopa-carbidopa 250/25 mg four times daily and entacapone 200 mg with each dose is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. The admitting team holds her Parkinson medications due to vomiting and being nil by mouth. On day 3 she develops high fevers, severe generalised rigidity, fluctuating consciousness, diaphoresis, and tachycardia.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128 bpm, BP 168/98 mmHg fluctuating, RR 26/min, T 40.2 C
data_table.Investigations: CK 8,400 U/L, WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, Cr 198 micromol/L (baseline 82), lactate 4.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most likely cause of this deterioration and the most appropriate intervention?

options.text: Septic shock from pneumonia - escalate antibiotics and commence IV vasopressors
Serotonin syndrome from antibiotic interaction - cease all serotonergic agents and give cyproheptadine
Malignant hyperthermia triggered by anaesthetic exposure during intubation procedures
Parkinson-hyperpyrexia syndrome - urgently reinstate dopaminergic medications via nasogastric tube
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome from newly commenced antiemetic - cease metoclopramide and give dantrolene

subtopic_detail: Vascular dementia vs Alzheimer disease discrimination
stem: A 76-year-old man is brought by his daughter for assessment of progressive cognitive decline over 12 months. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes, atrial fibrillation, and a previous lacunar stroke 2 years ago. His daughter reports his memory decline occurred in distinct steps rather than gradually, with a noticeable worsening after each episode of transient confusion. He has prominent executive dysfunction and psychomotor slowing but relatively preserved episodic memory in the early stages.

data_table.Investigations: MMSE 22/30, MoCA 18/30 (significant executive impairment), MRI brain shows multiple lacunar infarcts in the basal ganglia and periventricular white matter with moderate small vessel disease
data_table.Medications: Apixaban 5 mg BD, metformin 1 g BD, perindopril 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Alzheimer disease with concurrent cerebrovascular disease and mixed pathology
Lewy body dementia with vascular comorbidity and parkinsonism overlap
Normal pressure hydrocephalus presenting with cognitive decline and gait disturbance
Frontotemporal dementia with executive dysfunction as the predominant cognitive domain
Vascular dementia secondary to cerebral small vessel disease and strategic infarcts

subtopic_detail: Cholinesterase inhibitor initiation criteria and monitoring in Alzheimer disease
stem: A 78-year-old woman is diagnosed with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease after comprehensive assessment including neuropsychological testing and MRI. Her MMSE is 20/30. She lives with her husband and manages most activities of daily living with some prompting. Her medical history includes stable angina, hypertension, and a permanent pacemaker inserted 4 years ago. Her resting HR is 62 bpm. Her current medications are aspirin 100 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg daily.

data_table.Investigations: ECG: ventricular paced rhythm, rate 62 bpm, no conduction abnormality on native beats
data_table.Medications: Aspirin 100 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological intervention for her cognitive decline?

options.text: Commence donepezil 5 mg daily and increase to 10 mg after 4 to 6 weeks if tolerated
Commence memantine 5 mg daily as first-line given the cardiac history and bradycardia risk
Commence rivastigmine transdermal patch to avoid gastrointestinal side effects of oral agents
Defer pharmacotherapy and commence a structured cognitive stimulation program as sole treatment
Commence combined donepezil 10 mg and memantine 10 mg from the outset for maximal benefit

subtopic_detail: Rapidly progressive dementia workup - CJD vs paraneoplastic vs autoimmune
stem: A 62-year-old previously well woman is referred urgently by her GP with a 6-week history of rapidly progressive cognitive decline, personality change, and myoclonic jerks. She was functioning normally 2 months ago. Over the past 2 weeks she has developed visual hallucinations, gait ataxia, and is now unable to care for herself. There is no relevant family history. MRI brain shows bilateral cortical and caudate DWI restriction. CSF protein is mildly elevated at 0.52 g/L with no cells.

data_table.Investigations: MRI: bilateral cortical ribboning and caudate head DWI restriction, EEG: periodic sharp wave complexes at 1 to 2 Hz, CSF: protein 0.52 g/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L, WCC 0, RCC 0

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and the most appropriate confirmatory investigation?

options.text: Autoimmune encephalitis - send CSF and serum anti-NMDAR and anti-LGI1 antibodies
Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease - send CSF RT-QuIC assay and 14-3-3 protein
Paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis - send anti-Hu and anti-CV2 antibodies and CT body
Hashimoto encephalopathy - send anti-TPO antibodies and commence a steroid trial
Whipple disease of the CNS - send CSF Tropheryma whipplei PCR and duodenal biopsy

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with a sudden-onset severe headache reaching maximal intensity within 60 seconds while showering. She describes it as the worst headache of her life. She has no neurological deficits on examination. A non-contrast CT brain performed within 2 hours of onset is reported as normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78 bpm, BP 142/88 mmHg, RR 16/min, T 36.9 C, GCS 15
data_table.Examination: No neck stiffness, no focal neurological deficit, fundoscopy normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Reassure that the normal CT excludes subarachnoid haemorrhage and discharge with follow-up
Perform MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imaging to exclude ischaemic stroke as the cause
Perform lumbar puncture looking for xanthochromia and elevated red blood cell count
Arrange CT angiography of the cerebral vessels to directly assess for aneurysm or vasospasm
Administer IV sumatriptan as a diagnostic and therapeutic trial for severe migraine headache

subtopic_detail: RCVS recognition and management after SAH exclusion
stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with her third thunderclap headache in 10 days, each triggered by Valsalva manoeuvre or sexual activity. She uses sumatriptan for migraine and takes a combined oral contraceptive pill. Non-contrast CT and lumbar puncture after the first episode were normal. CT angiography now shows segmental narrowing of bilateral middle cerebral and posterior cerebral arteries in a string-of-beads pattern.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82 bpm, BP 148/92 mmHg, RR 14/min, T 36.7 C
data_table.Investigations: CT brain: no haemorrhage or infarct, CTA: multifocal segmental vasoconstriction bilateral MCA and PCA territories, LP (day 1): no xanthochromia, opening pressure 16 cmH2O

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence oral nimodipine and monitor for delayed cerebral infarction over the coming weeks
Perform urgent conventional cerebral angiography to plan endovascular vasodilator therapy
Commence high-dose IV methylprednisolone for presumed primary CNS vasculitis
Cease sumatriptan and the combined oral contraceptive and prescribe supportive analgesia only
Commence therapeutic anticoagulation with heparin to prevent stroke from the vasoconstriction

subtopic_detail: Massive transfusion protocol activation and component ratios
stem: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed motor vehicle collision. He has an obvious open femoral fracture and a rigid distended abdomen. Despite 2 litres of IV crystalloid his blood pressure remains 72/40 mmHg. The trauma team activates the massive transfusion protocol. O-negative packed red blood cells are being administered.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132 bpm, BP 72/40 mmHg (after 2 L crystalloid), RR 30/min, SpO2 94% on 15 L non-rebreather, T 35.2 C
data_table.Investigations: Hb 68 g/L, platelets 112 x10^9/L, INR 1.6, fibrinogen 1.1 g/L, lactate 6.8 mmol/L, pH 7.18

lead_in: What is the most appropriate blood product ratio to guide ongoing resuscitation?

options.text: Packed red blood cells alone until haemoglobin exceeds 100 g/L then reassess coagulation
Packed red cells and fresh frozen plasma in a ratio of 4:1 with platelets only if count drops below 50
Packed red cells and cryoprecipitate only, withholding FFP due to the risk of transfusion reactions
IV tranexamic acid 1 g and crystalloid only until crossmatched blood is available for transfusion
Packed red cells, FFP, and platelets in a 1:1:1 ratio with cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen falls below 1.5 g/L

subtopic_detail: Citrate toxicity and hypocalcaemia during massive transfusion
stem: A 28-year-old woman is undergoing massive transfusion for a ruptured ectopic pregnancy with estimated blood loss exceeding 4 litres. She has now received 10 units of packed red cells, 10 units of FFP, and 2 pooled doses of platelets over 90 minutes. The surgical team reports ongoing haemorrhage. She develops perioral paraesthesia, carpopedal spasm in her free hand, and the ECG monitor shows a prolonged QTc of 520 ms with new ST depression.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118 bpm, BP 92/58 mmHg, RR 24/min, T 34.8 C
data_table.Investigations: Ionised calcium 0.78 mmol/L (reference 1.12 to 1.32), K 5.9 mmol/L, pH 7.22, lactate 5.4 mmol/L, fibrinogen 0.9 g/L, INR 1.8

lead_in: What is the most likely cause of the QTc prolongation and the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Citrate toxicity causing hypocalcaemia - administer 10 mL of 10% calcium chloride IV over 10 minutes
Hyperkalaemia from stored red cell potassium leakage - administer IV calcium gluconate and insulin-dextrose
Hypothermia-induced cardiac instability - commence active external rewarming before any electrolyte correction
Dilutional coagulopathy causing myocardial ischaemia - administer cryoprecipitate and fresh frozen plasma
Transfusion-related acute lung injury causing hypoxic cardiac strain - cease transfusion and give IV furosemide

subtopic_detail: Sickle cell vaso-occlusive crisis - exchange transfusion indications
stem: A 24-year-old man with known HbSS sickle cell disease presents with severe bilateral lower limb and back pain consistent with a vaso-occlusive crisis. He is being managed with IV morphine patient-controlled analgesia, IV fluids, and supplemental oxygen. On day 2 of admission he develops acute right-sided hemiplegia with expressive aphasia. His baseline Hb is typically 80 to 90 g/L and his current Hb is 72 g/L with HbS fraction 78%.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 112 bpm, BP 148/88 mmHg, RR 20/min, SpO2 96% on 4 L nasal prongs, T 38.2 C
data_table.Investigations: Hb 72 g/L, HbS 78%, reticulocytes 280 x10^9/L, LDH 620 U/L, bilirubin 68 micromol/L, CT brain: no haemorrhage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention for this complication?

options.text: Commence IV alteplase at standard stroke dose given the CT excludes intracranial haemorrhage
Arrange urgent automated red cell exchange transfusion targeting HbS fraction below 30%
Perform simple top-up transfusion to raise Hb to 100 g/L and reassess neurological status
Commence therapeutic anticoagulation with IV heparin for presumed large vessel occlusion
Administer IV dexamethasone to reduce cerebral oedema and refer for urgent thrombectomy

subtopic_detail: Acute splenic sequestration crisis in adult HbSC disease
stem: A 22-year-old woman with known HbSC disease presents with sudden-onset left upper quadrant pain, nausea, and light-headedness. She has had no prior splenic complications. Her baseline Hb is typically 110 g/L. On examination she appears pale and diaphoretic. Her spleen is palpable 6 cm below the left costal margin, which is new from her last clinic visit 3 months ago where the spleen was not palpable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128 bpm, BP 82/52 mmHg, RR 24/min, SpO2 92% on room air, T 37.6 C
data_table.Investigations: Hb 52 g/L (baseline 110), reticulocytes 420 x10^9/L, platelets 68 x10^9/L (baseline 220), LDH 890 U/L, bilirubin 82 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Splenic infarction with haemolytic crisis - commence IV fluids and simple red cell transfusion
Hypersplenism from chronic congestion - arrange elective splenectomy within the coming weeks
Acute splenic sequestration - commence cautious transfusion targeting Hb 80 to 90 g/L and plan splenectomy
Aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19 - check parvovirus serology and transfuse to baseline Hb
Haemolytic crisis with DIC - commence exchange transfusion and IV heparin for coagulopathy

subtopic_detail: ABG interpretation - mixed acid-base disorder identification
stem: A 52-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and COPD presents with 3 days of vomiting, polyuria, and increasing confusion. He has been unable to take his metformin or fluids for 3 days. He appears dehydrated with Kussmaul breathing.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 112 bpm, BP 96/62 mmHg, RR 32/min deep, SpO2 94% on room air, T 37.2 C
data_table.Investigations: ABG: pH 7.18, pCO2 22 mmHg, pO2 92 mmHg, HCO3 8 mmol/L, BE -18. Na 138 mmol/L, K 5.8 mmol/L, Cl 98 mmol/L, BSL 38.2 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L, Cr 248 micromol/L, urea 22 mmol/L

lead_in: Which acid-base disturbance is present?

options.text: Simple high anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation only
High anion gap metabolic acidosis with concurrent respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation
High anion gap metabolic acidosis with concurrent non-anion gap metabolic acidosis from renal impairment
High anion gap metabolic acidosis with concurrent metabolic alkalosis suggested by the delta-delta ratio
Mixed respiratory acidosis and high anion gap metabolic acidosis from COPD and diabetic ketoacidosis

subtopic_detail: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with osmolal gap - toxic alcohol
stem: A 45-year-old man is found confused in a park and brought to the emergency department by ambulance. He smells of alcohol. He is unable to provide a history. On examination he has nystagmus, ataxia, and appears intoxicated but there is no focal neurological deficit. His serum ethanol level returns as undetectable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 98 bpm, BP 108/68 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 97% on room air, T 36.4 C
data_table.Investigations: ABG: pH 7.12, pCO2 18 mmHg, HCO3 6 mmol/L. Na 140 mmol/L, K 4.8 mmol/L, Cl 102 mmol/L, BSL 5.4 mmol/L, ketones 0.4 mmol/L, Cr 188 micromol/L, measured serum osmolality 326 mOsm/kg, calculated osmolality 289 mOsm/kg, urine microscopy: envelope-shaped crystals

lead_in: What is the most likely cause and the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Methanol poisoning - commence IV ethanol infusion and arrange urgent haemodialysis
Isopropanol ingestion - provide supportive care as this does not cause significant acidosis
Starvation ketoacidosis - administer IV dextrose and thiamine and reassess in 4 hours
Ethylene glycol poisoning - administer IV fomepizole and arrange urgent haemodialysis
Ethylene glycol poisoning - commence IV fomepizole and simultaneous urgent haemodialysis

subtopic_detail: Lung cancer screening eligibility and LDCT referral
stem: A 58-year-old man presents for a routine health assessment. He has a 40-pack-year smoking history and quit smoking 8 years ago. He has no respiratory symptoms. He asks about lung cancer screening after seeing a media report about the Australian lung cancer screening program.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 72 bpm, BP 132/82 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Examination: Normal respiratory examination, no clubbing, no lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response regarding lung cancer screening eligibility?

options.text: He is eligible for biennial LDCT screening under the National Lung Cancer Screening Program
He is ineligible because he quit smoking more than 5 years ago and his risk has normalised
He should have an annual chest X-ray as the recommended initial lung cancer screening modality
He should undergo sputum cytology combined with spirometry as the recommended screening pathway
He is ineligible because screening is only offered to current smokers with active respiratory symptoms

subtopic_detail: Incidental lung mass urgent referral and staging workup
stem: A 64-year-old woman who is a current smoker (45 pack-years) presents with a 6-week history of persistent cough, haemoptysis, and unintentional weight loss of 4 kg. A chest X-ray shows a 3.5 cm spiculated mass in the right upper lobe with ipsilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. She has no prior imaging for comparison.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82 bpm, BP 128/78 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 96% on room air
data_table.Investigations: CXR: 3.5 cm spiculated RUL mass with right hilar lymphadenopathy, FBC and UEC normal, calcium 2.82 mmol/L (corrected), LDH 310 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in the investigation pathway?

options.text: Refer for CT-guided percutaneous biopsy of the lung mass before any further imaging
Arrange urgent contrast CT chest and upper abdomen and refer to a multidisciplinary lung cancer team
Commence empiric antibiotics for 6 weeks to exclude an infective cause before further workup
Arrange PET-CT as the first investigation to determine metabolic activity and distant metastases
Repeat the chest X-ray in 6 weeks to assess for interval growth before proceeding with CT

subtopic_detail: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cardiovascular risk assessment
stem: A 38-year-old Aboriginal man presents to his Aboriginal Medical Service for a routine health check. He has no known medical conditions and takes no medications. He smokes 15 cigarettes per day. His father died of a myocardial infarction at age 42. He works as a mechanic and has a sedentary lifestyle outside work.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78 bpm, BP 138/88 mmHg, BMI 31 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Total cholesterol 5.8 mmol/L, LDL 3.6 mmol/L, HDL 0.9 mmol/L, triglycerides 2.4 mmol/L, BSL fasting 5.8 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.9%, eGFR 88 mL/min/1.73m2, ACR 4.2 mg/mmol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to cardiovascular risk assessment in this patient?

options.text: Apply the standard Framingham risk equation and treat only if the 10-year risk exceeds 15%
Defer formal risk assessment until age 45 as recommended for the general male population
Classify as high cardiovascular risk given Aboriginal status with multiple risk factors and treat accordingly
Calculate his absolute risk using the standard Australian calculator and treat based on that result only
Focus exclusively on lifestyle modification for 12 months before considering pharmacotherapy

subtopic_detail: Rheumatic heart disease screening and secondary prophylaxis in Aboriginal communities
stem: A 14-year-old Aboriginal girl from a remote Northern Territory community presents with her third episode of acute rheumatic fever. She was diagnosed with her first episode at age 8 and has been on secondary prophylaxis with intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin but has missed several doses due to difficulties accessing the clinic. Echocardiography performed today shows moderate mitral regurgitation with mild mitral stenosis. Her cardiac function is preserved.

data_table.Investigations: Echocardiography: moderate MR with mild MS, LA mildly dilated, LVEF 58%, no aortic valve involvement, ESR 48 mm/hr, ASO titre 640 IU/mL (elevated)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate duration of secondary prophylaxis for this patient?

options.text: Continue IM benzathine benzylpenicillin every 4 weeks until age 21 then cease prophylaxis entirely
Switch to oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 250 mg twice daily as it is easier to adhere to than injections
Cease prophylaxis as three episodes of ARF indicate treatment failure and surgery is now required
Continue IM benzathine benzylpenicillin every 4 weeks until age 40 or for 10 years after last ARF episode
Continue prophylaxis for life given the severity of her rheumatic heart disease and recurrence pattern

subtopic_detail: Infective endocarditis surgical indications - heart failure with severe regurgitation
stem: A 52-year-old man with native aortic valve infective endocarditis caused by Staphylococcus aureus is on day 5 of appropriate IV antibiotics. He was initially stable but has developed progressive dyspnoea and orthopnoea over 48 hours. Repeat echocardiography shows severe aortic regurgitation with a mobile 14 mm vegetation on the aortic valve. He has elevated JVP, bilateral basal crepitations, and a new early diastolic murmur.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108 bpm, BP 118/42 mmHg (wide pulse pressure), RR 28/min, SpO2 92% on 6 L face mask, T 37.8 C
data_table.Investigations: BNP 1,840 ng/L, Hb 108 g/L, WCC 16.2 x10^9/L, CRP 128 mg/L, blood cultures day 3: S. aureus (now on appropriate antibiotics)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue IV antibiotics for the full 6-week course and manage heart failure with IV diuretics only
Switch to broader-spectrum antibiotics assuming treatment failure and reassess in 48 hours
Commence IV sodium nitroprusside to reduce afterload and defer surgery until infection is controlled
Arrange percutaneous aortic valve replacement as a less invasive alternative to open surgery
Refer urgently for aortic valve replacement surgery while continuing IV antibiotics perioperatively

subtopic_detail: Infective endocarditis with perivalvular abscess and conduction abnormality
stem: A 48-year-old man with prosthetic aortic valve endocarditis caused by Enterococcus faecalis is on day 10 of IV ampicillin and gentamicin. He has been febrile intermittently despite appropriate antibiotics. His daily ECG today shows a new first-degree AV block with PR interval of 280 ms that was not present on admission. A transthoracic echocardiogram is technically limited due to prosthetic valve acoustic shadowing.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 68 bpm, BP 126/72 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, T 38.4 C
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus rhythm, PR 280 ms (admission PR 160 ms), WCC 14.8 x10^9/L, CRP 96 mg/L (down from 180 on admission), blood cultures day 8: sterile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Transoesophageal echocardiography to assess for perivalvular abscess and paravalvular leak
Cardiac MRI with gadolinium to characterise the myocardial tissue around the prosthetic valve
Repeat transthoracic echocardiogram in 1 week as the TTE limitation is likely to resolve with fasting
24-hour Holter monitor to characterise the degree of conduction disease before any further imaging
Electrophysiology study to assess the level of AV block and need for permanent pacemaker insertion

subtopic_detail: Bacterial meningitis empiric therapy and adjunctive dexamethasone
stem: A 52-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of worsening headache, fever, and neck stiffness. His wife reports he has become increasingly confused over the past 3 hours. He has no significant past medical history and takes no regular medications. He is not immunocompromised and has no history of recent neurosurgery or head trauma.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4, HR 112, BP 135/82, RR 22, SpO2 96% on room air, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6)
data_table.Examination: Marked neck stiffness, positive Kernig sign, no focal neurological deficits, no papilloedema on fundoscopy, no rash
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.2 x10^9/L (neutrophils 15.8), CRP 245 mg/L, lactate 2.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: IV dexamethasone followed by IV ceftriaxone within 20 minutes
Urgent CT brain followed by lumbar puncture before starting antibiotics
IV benzylpenicillin followed by urgent lumbar puncture
IV ceftriaxone and IV vancomycin without dexamethasone
IV ceftriaxone and IV metronidazole with dexamethasone

subtopic_detail: HSV encephalitis recognition and empiric aciclovir
stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of headache, fever, and personality change. Her partner reports she has been unusually irritable and had a brief episode of olfactory hallucinations yesterday. She has no past psychiatric history. On examination she is febrile, disoriented to time and place, but follows simple commands. There are no focal motor deficits and no meningism.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9, HR 98, BP 128/76, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6)
data_table.Investigations: WCC 11.4 x10^9/L, CRP 48 mg/L, CT brain with contrast shows subtle low density in the left temporal lobe
data_table.CSF: Opening pressure 22 cmH2O, WCC 85 (lymphocyte-predominant), protein 0.9 g/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L (serum 5.8 mmol/L), Gram stain negative

lead_in: What is the single most important next step in management?

options.text: Arrange urgent MRI brain and await results before initiating treatment
Commence IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly without awaiting PCR results
Start IV ceftriaxone and dexamethasone for possible meningitis
Send CSF for HSV PCR and start treatment once result is positive
Commence oral valaciclovir 1 g 8-hourly with outpatient follow-up

subtopic_detail: Cushing syndrome screening with overnight dexamethasone suppression test
stem: A 45-year-old woman is referred by her GP for investigation of possible Cushing syndrome. She has gained 12 kg over the past 18 months with central adiposity, developed facial plethora, and has new-onset hypertension requiring two agents. She also reports easy bruising and proximal muscle weakness. She takes amlodipine 10 mg daily and perindopril 5 mg daily. She does not take any glucocorticoid medications or herbal supplements. An overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test returns a morning serum cortisol of 290 nmol/L.

data_table.Examination: Central obesity, moon facies, dorsal fat pad, thin skin with ecchymoses on forearms, proximal lower limb weakness (MRC grade 4)
data_table.Investigations: Fasting BSL 7.8 mmol/L, HbA1c 6.8%, K+ 3.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in this patient's evaluation?

options.text: Proceed directly to CT adrenal glands to identify the source
Repeat the overnight dexamethasone suppression test to confirm the result
Measure 24-hour urinary free cortisol to confirm hypercortisolism
Measure serum ACTH to differentiate ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent causes
Refer for inferior petrosal sinus sampling to localise the source

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis management in known primary adrenal insufficiency
stem: A 34-year-old woman with known Addison disease on hydrocortisone 20 mg mane and 10 mg nocte replacement presents to the emergency department after 48 hours of vomiting and diarrhoea from a gastroenteritis illness. She has been unable to keep her oral hydrocortisone down for the past 24 hours. She is visibly unwell and drowsy. Her husband confirms she carries a steroid emergency card and intramuscular hydrocortisone injection kit but neither was used at home.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.2, HR 128, BP 78/48 (supine), RR 24, SpO2 97% on room air, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6)
data_table.Investigations: Na+ 126 mmol/L, K+ 6.2 mmol/L, urea 14.2 mmol/L, creatinine 148 micromol/L, BSL 2.8 mmol/L, venous pH 7.28, lactate 4.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IV normal saline 1 L stat followed by oral fludrocortisone 100 mcg
IV dexamethasone 4 mg stat and IV 5% dextrose 500 mL stat
IM hydrocortisone 100 mg stat and arrange outpatient review in 24 hours
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 50 mg IV 6-hourly with IV normal saline
IV prednisolone 50 mg stat then 25 mg 12-hourly with IV Hartmann solution

stem: A 41-year-old man is investigated for episodic headaches, palpitations, and diaphoresis. He was found to have severe paroxysmal hypertension (240/130 mmHg) during one episode in the emergency department. Twenty-four-hour urine fractionated metanephrines are markedly elevated, and CT abdomen reveals a 4 cm right adrenal mass with avid contrast enhancement. He is referred for laparoscopic adrenalectomy. He currently takes no regular medications. His resting heart rate between episodes is 62 bpm.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 152/96 (between episodes), HR 62, RR 16
data_table.Investigations: 24-hour urine normetanephrine 8400 nmol (ref < 900), metanephrine 3200 nmol (ref < 1800), fasting BSL 6.4 mmol/L, calcium 2.48 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate preoperative pharmacological preparation?

options.text: Start metoprolol 25 mg twice daily and up-titrate to control heart rate
Start amlodipine 10 mg daily as the sole preoperative antihypertensive agent
Start phenoxybenzamine and atenolol simultaneously for dual blockade
Start prazosin and schedule surgery within 48 hours to minimise risk
Start phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily and titrate over 10-14 days with salt loading

subtopic_detail: Synacthen test interpretation in suspected primary adrenal insufficiency
stem: A 29-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of progressive fatigue, weight loss of 8 kg, and intermittent nausea. She has noticed darkening of her skin creases and buccal mucosa over the past 3 months. She takes no medications. A short Synacthen test is performed. Her baseline 0900h cortisol is 85 nmol/L, and her 30-minute post-Synacthen cortisol is 180 nmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 98/62 supine, 82/54 standing, HR 96, BMI 19.5
data_table.Investigations: Na+ 131 mmol/L, K+ 5.6 mmol/L, urea 8.4 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, TSH 5.8 mIU/L, fT4 10.2 pmol/L, BSL 3.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation and next investigation?

options.text: Failed Synacthen test confirming adrenal insufficiency; measure serum ACTH to determine aetiology
Borderline Synacthen result; repeat the test in 4 weeks with concurrent ACTH stimulation
Normal Synacthen response; investigate alternative causes of fatigue and weight loss
Failed Synacthen test; proceed directly to CT adrenal glands for structural assessment
Failed Synacthen test; start hydrocortisone and measure 21-hydroxylase antibodies as the sole investigation

subtopic_detail: Guillain-Barre syndrome respiratory monitoring and treatment
stem: A 48-year-old man presents with 4 days of progressive ascending weakness affecting both legs, now involving his hands. He reports paraesthesiae in his feet preceding the weakness by 2 days. He had a campylobacter gastroenteritis 2 weeks ago. On examination, reflexes are absent throughout and he has bilateral facial weakness. He can walk with assistance but has difficulty rising from a chair. His forced vital capacity is 2.1 L (predicted 4.2 L).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84, BP 148/92, RR 20, SpO2 96% on room air
data_table.Examination: MRC grade 3 hip flexion, grade 4- knee extension, grade 4- wrist extension, bilateral facial weakness, areflexia throughout, no sensory level
data_table.Investigations: CSF protein 1.2 g/L, CSF WCC 2 cells/microL, nerve conduction studies show demyelinating pattern

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Start oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily and monitor FVC 4-hourly on the ward
Commence IV immunoglobulin 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days and transfer to ICU for FVC monitoring
Arrange urgent plasma exchange followed by IV immunoglobulin for combined therapy
Start oral mycophenolate mofetil and monitor on the general neurology ward
Commence IV immunoglobulin 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days and monitor on the general ward

subtopic_detail: Miller Fisher syndrome recognition and anti-GQ1b antibody
stem: A 36-year-old man presents with 3 days of progressive double vision and unsteady gait following a recent upper respiratory tract infection. He reports no limb weakness or numbness. On examination he has bilateral ptosis, complete external ophthalmoplegia, and wide-based ataxic gait. Limb power is full (MRC 5/5 throughout) and sensory examination is normal. Deep tendon reflexes are absent throughout.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76, BP 122/78, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Bilateral ptosis, complete external ophthalmoplegia, normal pupils, wide-based cerebellar-type ataxia, areflexia, full limb power, normal sensation
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain normal, CSF protein 0.6 g/L with WCC 1 cell/microL

lead_in: Which antibody test would most strongly support the suspected diagnosis?

options.text: Anti-acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibody testing
Anti-neuronal nuclear antibody (ANNA-1/anti-Hu)
Anti-GQ1b ganglioside antibody panel testing
Anti-MuSK (muscle-specific kinase) antibody testing
Anti-aquaporin-4 (anti-AQP4) antibody testing

subtopic_detail: Myasthenia gravis crisis and medication avoidance
stem: A 62-year-old woman with known generalised myasthenia gravis on pyridostigmine 60 mg four times daily and prednisolone 15 mg daily presents with worsening dyspnoea and difficulty swallowing over 3 days. She had been recently treated by her GP for a urinary tract infection. On examination she has bilateral ptosis, nasal speech, weak cough, and neck flexion weakness. Her FVC is 1.1 L (predicted 2.8 L).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 138/84, RR 24, SpO2 94% on room air
data_table.Examination: Bilateral ptosis, nasal speech, weak palatal movement, weak cough, neck flexion MRC grade 3
data_table.Medications: Pyridostigmine 60 mg QID, prednisolone 15 mg daily, gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV daily (started 2 days ago)

lead_in: What is the single most important initial intervention?

options.text: Increase pyridostigmine to 90 mg four times daily and monitor clinically
Start IV immunoglobulin 0.4 g/kg/day immediately and continue current antibiotics
Administer IV edrophonium to differentiate myasthenic from cholinergic crisis
Cease gentamicin immediately and substitute a non-aminoglycoside antibiotic
Intubate immediately for airway protection and commence plasma exchange

subtopic_detail: Motor neuron disease recognition and initial investigation
stem:
A 58-year-old man is referred with a 9-month history of progressive weakness affecting his right hand, making it difficult to use his keys and button his shirt. Over the past 3 months he has also noticed his right foot catching on the ground when walking. He has lost 6 kg. His wife has noticed occasional slurred speech but no swallowing difficulty.

He has no sensory symptoms, no bladder dysfunction, and no pain. On examination, there is wasting of the right hand intrinsics and right tibialis anterior. Fasciculations are visible in both upper limbs and the tongue.

data_table.Examination: Wasting right first dorsal interosseous and thenar eminence, fasciculations bilateral deltoids and biceps plus tongue, right foot drop, brisk reflexes throughout including jaw jerk, upgoing plantar responses bilaterally, no sensory deficit, normal eye movements
data_table.Investigations: MRI cervical and thoracic spine shows no compressive lesion, B12 560 pmol/L, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, CK mildly elevated at 420 U/L

lead_in: What investigation would best support the suspected diagnosis?

options.text: Lumbar puncture with CSF analysis including oligoclonal bands
Anti-acetylcholine receptor and anti-MuSK antibody testing
Genetic testing for hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy
MRI brain with gadolinium focusing on the posterior fossa
Electromyography and nerve conduction studies across multiple regions

subtopic_detail: Acute pericarditis diagnosis and treatment with colchicine
stem: A 27-year-old man presents with 2 days of sharp central chest pain that worsens on inspiration and lying flat and improves when sitting forward. He had a viral upper respiratory tract infection 10 days ago. He has no significant past medical history. His troponin I is 28 ng/L (reference less than 26) and his ECG shows widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression in limb leads.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6, HR 88, BP 118/74, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Pericardial friction rub on auscultation, no signs of heart failure, JVP not elevated
data_table.Investigations: CRP 62 mg/L, troponin I 28 ng/L (ref < 26), echocardiogram shows trivial pericardial effusion with normal LV function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily plus colchicine 500 mcg twice daily for 3 months
Prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg daily tapering over 4 weeks as first-line therapy
Aspirin 900 mg three times daily without colchicine and activity restriction for 6 weeks
Dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel for suspected ACS
Pericardiocentesis to drain the effusion and relieve tamponade physiology

subtopic_detail: Acute myocarditis with heart failure and CMR role
stem: A 31-year-old man presents with 5 days of progressive dyspnoea and a 1-day history of orthopnoea. He reports a febrile illness with myalgia 2 weeks ago. He has no cardiac history. His ECG shows sinus tachycardia with non-specific ST-T changes. Serial troponin I levels are 1840 ng/L and 1920 ng/L (reference less than 26). Coronary angiography shows normal coronary arteries.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8, HR 112, BP 102/68, RR 24, SpO2 93% on 4 L nasal prongs
data_table.Examination: Elevated JVP, bibasal crackles, S3 gallop, no murmurs, mild peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: BNP 1240 pg/mL, CRP 88 mg/L, echocardiogram shows globally reduced LV function with EF 28%, no regional wall motion abnormalities, trivial pericardial effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Repeat echocardiography in 48 hours to assess for interval change
Cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement and T2 mapping
Endomyocardial biopsy from the right ventricle via femoral vein
CT coronary angiography to exclude subtle coronary artery disease
Viral serology panel including coxsackie B, adenovirus, and parvovirus B19

stem: A 68-year-old woman is investigated for a moderate right-sided pleural effusion. She has a history of congestive heart failure. A diagnostic thoracentesis is performed.

data_table.Pleural fluid: Appearance: straw-coloured, pH 7.38, protein 42 g/L, LDH 280 U/L, glucose 4.8 mmol/L, WCC 650 cells/microL (lymphocyte-predominant)
data_table.Serum: Protein 65 g/L, LDH 180 U/L, albumin 32 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.text: Transudative effusion consistent with heart failure; optimise diuretics
Exudative effusion; start empiric antibiotics for parapneumonic cause
Exudative effusion; send pleural fluid for cytology and consider CT thorax with contrast
Borderline effusion; repeat thoracentesis in 2 weeks after optimising diuretics
Exudative effusion; perform therapeutic drainage and discharge for GP follow-up

subtopic_detail: Type A vs Type B aortic dissection management
stem: A 62-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension presents with sudden-onset severe tearing chest pain radiating to his back. He is diaphoretic. His blood pressure is markedly different between arms. CT aortogram reveals an intimal flap originating in the ascending aorta and extending into the descending thoracic aorta. There is no pericardial effusion and his aortic valve is competent.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 104, BP 198/112 right arm, 152/88 left arm, RR 22, SpO2 95% on room air
data_table.Investigations: CT aortogram: intimal flap arising 3 cm above the aortic valve extending through the arch into the descending thoracic aorta (Stanford Type A), true lumen patent, no malperfusion, no pericardial effusion
data_table.Examination: Equal femoral pulses, no new murmur, no focal neurology

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management approach?

options.text: IV nitroprusside infusion to target systolic BP below 120 mmHg and surgical consultation
IV esmolol infusion targeting HR below 60 and manage medically with serial CT surveillance
Emergency endovascular thoracic stent-graft repair as the primary intervention
IV hydralazine to achieve rapid BP control and monitor in ICU for 72 hours before deciding on surgery
IV esmolol infusion targeting HR below 60 and SBP 100-120 mmHg with emergency open surgical repair

subtopic_detail: TEN management and SCORTEN prognostic scoring
stem: A 55-year-old woman is transferred to the burns unit with progressive painful erythroderma and skin detachment over 4 days. She was started on allopurinol 6 weeks ago for recurrent gout. On admission, greater than 40% of her body surface area shows full-thickness epidermal detachment with positive Nikolsky sign. Her mucous membranes are severely involved with haemorrhagic crusting of the lips and bilateral conjunctival pseudomembrane formation. She is oliguric.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6, HR 118, BP 92/58, RR 26, SpO2 92% on 6 L nasal prongs
data_table.Investigations: Na+ 132 mmol/L, K+ 4.8 mmol/L, urea 18.4 mmol/L, creatinine 186 micromol/L, BSL 14.2 mmol/L, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, albumin 22 g/L, WCC 2.8 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most important immediate management priority alongside fluid resuscitation?

options.text: Cease allopurinol permanently and initiate wound care in a burns unit environment
Start IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily pulse therapy for 3 consecutive days
Administer IV immunoglobulin 3 g/kg total dose over 3-4 consecutive days
Commence oral ciclosporin 3 mg/kg daily as the primary disease-modifying agent
Apply silver sulfadiazine to affected areas and arrange outpatient dermatology review

stem: A 74-year-old man on warfarin for mechanical mitral valve replacement presents with large-volume haematemesis. He is haemodynamically unstable. His INR returns at 8.2. Gastroscopy is planned urgently once coagulation is corrected.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 88/54, RR 24, SpO2 94% on room air
data_table.Investigations: INR 8.2, Hb 72 g/L (baseline 132), platelets 188 x10^9/L, fibrinogen 2.8 g/L
data_table.Medications: Warfarin 6 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate coagulation reversal strategy?

options.text: IV vitamin K 10 mg alone and recheck INR in 6 hours before proceeding
IV prothrombinex-VF 50 IU/kg plus IV vitamin K 5 mg and packed red cell transfusion
Fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg and IV vitamin K 1 mg with blood group crossmatch
Recombinant factor VIIa 90 mcg/kg IV as a single dose with oral vitamin K 10 mg
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV plus cryoprecipitate 10 units and withhold further warfarin

stem: A 42-year-old woman is referred for investigation of possible Cushing syndrome. She has a 12-month history of central weight gain, easy bruising, and proximal muscle weakness. She also reports new-onset hypertension and irregular menses. Her GP performed an overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 156/94 mmHg, HR 78/min, BMI 34 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: Central adiposity, moon facies, dorsal fat pad, purple striae on abdomen, proximal weakness grade 4/5
data_table.Investigations: 1 mg DST morning cortisol: 80 nmol/L (suppress below 50); fasting glucose 7.8 mmol/L; K+ 3.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Late-night salivary cortisol on two separate occasions
High-dose 8 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test
Inferior petrosal sinus sampling with CRH stimulation
CT adrenal glands with IV contrast and thin slices
Pituitary MRI with gadolinium and dynamic sequences

stem: A 48-year-old man presents to a hypertension clinic after his GP identified resistant hypertension on three agents. He has no significant past history other than occasional muscle cramps. Medications include amlodipine 10 mg daily, perindopril 10 mg daily, and indapamide 2.5 mg daily. The indapamide was ceased 6 weeks ago and perindopril was switched to verapamil for screening purposes.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 162/98 mmHg, HR 72/min
data_table.Investigations: K+ 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); Na+ 142 mmol/L; creatinine 78 micromol/L; aldosterone 620 pmol/L (reference 100-450); direct renin concentration 3 mU/L (reference 10-50); ARR 207

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence spironolactone 25 mg daily and repeat ARR in 6 weeks
Arrange a saline suppression test to confirm autonomous aldosterone
Request bilateral adrenal vein sampling with cosyntropin infusion
Request CT adrenal glands to identify a unilateral adenoma
Repeat the aldosterone-to-renin ratio after a further 6 weeks

stem: A 56-year-old woman on long-term prednisolone 15 mg daily for polymyalgia rheumatica presents to the emergency department with 2 days of vomiting, diarrhoea, and progressive lethargy after a gastroenteritis illness. She has been unable to take her oral prednisolone for the past 48 hours. She appears profoundly unwell.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8 C, HR 122/min, BP 74/42 mmHg (unresponsive to 1 L crystalloid), RR 22/min, SpO2 97% on room air
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, dry mucous membranes, diffuse abdominal tenderness, hyperpigmented palmar creases
data_table.Investigations: Na+ 128 mmol/L; K+ 5.8 mmol/L; glucose 3.1 mmol/L; creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 68); cortisol 42 nmol/L (taken at 0800)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Send a cosyntropin stimulation test then await results to guide dosing
Commence IV dexamethasone 4 mg and oral fludrocortisone 100 mcg
Administer IV noradrenaline infusion and broad-spectrum antibiotics
Administer IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat and IV normal saline bolus
Resume oral prednisolone 15 mg with IV ondansetron and oral rehydration

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with a 5-day history of left-sided optic neuritis confirmed on ophthalmology review. She has no prior neurological symptoms. MRI brain shows the symptomatic left optic nerve lesion plus three periventricular white matter lesions and one juxtacortical lesion, all enhancing with gadolinium. MRI spinal cord shows a single non-enhancing thoracic cord lesion. Lumbar puncture reveals oligoclonal bands present in CSF but absent in serum.

data_table.Investigations: MRI brain: left optic nerve enhancement, 3 periventricular lesions (enhancing), 1 juxtacortical lesion (enhancing); MRI spine: 1 thoracic cord lesion (non-enhancing); CSF: oligoclonal bands positive; serum oligoclonal bands negative; VEP: delayed left P100

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnostic conclusion and next step?

options.text: Diagnosis of MS is met and referral for disease-modifying therapy
Clinically isolated syndrome requiring a second clinical event
Probable MS requiring repeat MRI in 3 months for new lesions
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder requiring aquaporin-4 testing
Isolated optic neuritis with incidental white matter changes

stem: A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance with a 2-day history of increasing confusion and urinary frequency. His wife reports he has been febrile at home. He has a past history of type 2 diabetes on metformin and benign prostatic hyperplasia.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.2 C, HR 118/min, BP 82/48 mmHg, RR 26/min, SpO2 94% on room air
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), suprapubic tenderness, no meningism, warm peripheries
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.29, lactate 4.8 mmol/L; BSL 14.2 mmol/L; urinalysis: leucocytes +++, nitrites positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management priority?

options.text: Insert an indwelling catheter and send urine for culture
Obtain blood cultures then commence empiric IV antibiotics
Commence IV noradrenaline infusion targeting MAP above 65
Request urgent CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
Administer IV insulin infusion targeting BSL below 10

stem: A 52-year-old right-handed accountant presents with an 18-month history of progressive left hand rest tremor, slowness buttoning his shirts, and reduced arm swing when walking. He has no cognitive complaints and continues to work full-time. General examination reveals mild left upper limb cogwheel rigidity and bradykinesia with reduced finger-tapping amplitude. MRI brain is unremarkable. He is diagnosed with early Parkinson disease and asks about treatment options.

data_table.Examination: Asymmetric left upper limb rest tremor (4-6 Hz), cogwheel rigidity left arm, bradykinesia left hand with decrement on repeated finger tapping, mildly reduced left arm swing, normal gait and balance, MMSE 30/30
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain: no structural lesion, no vascular changes; DaTscan: reduced left putaminal uptake

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Levodopa-carbidopa 100/25 mg three times daily as first-line
Selegiline 5 mg twice daily as a neuroprotective monotherapy
Pramipexole titrated from 0.125 mg three times daily upward
Benzhexol 2 mg three times daily for the prominent tremor
Amantadine 100 mg twice daily as an initial monotherapy agent

stem: A 58-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of severe headache, fever, and progressive confusion. He has no significant past history and takes no regular medications. On examination he is febrile with marked neck stiffness and a positive Kernig sign. CT brain shows no mass lesion or hydrocephalus. Lumbar puncture is performed.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.6 C, HR 108/min, BP 148/82 mmHg, RR 20/min, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6)
data_table.Investigations: CSF: WCC 1840 cells/microL (95% neutrophils); protein 3.2 g/L; glucose 1.1 mmol/L (paired serum glucose 7.8 mmol/L); Gram stain: gram-positive diplococci

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric antimicrobial regimen?

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly alone commenced after CSF results
IV vancomycin and IV meropenem with oral dexamethasone daily
IV flucloxacillin and IV gentamicin with IV dexamethasone
IV ceftriaxone, IV benzylpenicillin, and IV dexamethasone
IV ceftriaxone and IV metronidazole with IV dexamethasone

stem: A 54-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents to the emergency department with a 24-hour history of rapidly worsening left lower leg pain and swelling following a minor gardening laceration 3 days ago. He reports the pain is severe and seems disproportionate to the visible skin changes. He has been febrile at home.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9 C, HR 112/min, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 22/min
data_table.Examination: Left lower leg erythema extending above the knee, tense oedema, skin dusky in patches, crepitus palpable over the mid-calf, pain on passive stretch of ankle, reduced sensation over the affected area
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L (neutrophils 19.8); CRP 312 mg/L; lactate 3.1 mmol/L; creatinine 128 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Arrange emergency surgical exploration and debridement now
Request urgent CT with IV contrast to delineate tissue planes
Commence IV flucloxacillin 2 g and elevate limb for 24 hours
Perform bedside needle aspiration of the affected soft tissue
Administer IV clindamycin and arrange MRI within 24 hours

stem: A 62-year-old woman with known seropositive myasthenia gravis on pyridostigmine and prednisolone presents with worsening dysphagia, nasal speech, and difficulty lifting her head off the pillow over the past 3 days. She recently completed a course of azithromycin for community-acquired pneumonia. She is sitting upright in bed and appears anxious with shallow breathing.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96/min, BP 142/78 mmHg, RR 24/min, SpO2 93% on room air
data_table.Examination: Bilateral ptosis, weak neck flexion (MRC grade 3/5), nasal speech, pooling of secretions, use of accessory muscles of respiration
data_table.Investigations: FVC 0.9 L (predicted 2.8 L - 32% predicted); ABG: pH 7.36, pCO2 52 mmHg, pO2 68 mmHg, HCO3 28 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most critical parameter to guide the decision for intubation?

options.text: Arterial blood gas pCO2 level repeated every 4 hours
Serial forced vital capacity measured every 2-4 hours
Continuous pulse oximetry with a target SpO2 above 94%
Peak expiratory flow rate measured twice daily at bedside
Repeat chest X-ray every 12 hours to assess for atelectasis

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to her GP with a 2-day history of dysuria, urinary frequency, and suprapubic discomfort. She is otherwise well with no fever or flank pain. She is not pregnant, has no drug allergies, and has normal renal function. Urine dipstick shows leucocytes 2+ and nitrites positive.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 C, HR 72/min, BP 118/72 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Mild suprapubic tenderness, no costovertebral angle tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick: leucocytes 2+, nitrites positive, blood 1+; eGFR 92 mL/min

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic?

options.text: Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days
Cefalexin 500 mg twice daily for 5 days total
Trimethoprim 300 mg once daily for 3 days total
Norfloxacin 400 mg twice daily for 3 days total
Nitrofurantoin 50 mg four times daily for 7 days

stem: A 38-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 4 days of progressive ascending weakness following a campylobacter gastroenteritis illness 2 weeks ago. He was initially unsteady on his feet and now cannot stand without assistance. He reports tingling in his hands and feet. He has no facial weakness or swallowing difficulty. Nerve conduction studies show demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 62/min (resting), BP 128/76 mmHg lying and 104/68 mmHg standing, RR 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Examination: MRC grade 3/5 hip flexion bilaterally, 4-/5 knee extension, 4/5 ankle dorsiflexion, absent ankle and knee reflexes, glove-and-stocking sensory loss to mid-shin, no facial weakness, intact swallow
data_table.Investigations: FVC 2.4 L (predicted 4.2 L - 57% predicted); CSF: protein 1.8 g/L, WCC 2 cells/microL, glucose 3.8 mmol/L (paired serum 5.2 mmol/L)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 14 days
Monitor FVC every 4 hours and treat only if below 15 mL/kg
Administer IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days
Commence IV immunoglobulin 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days
Arrange urgent plasma exchange for 5 sessions over 10 days

stem: A 72-year-old man presents to the emergency department within 2 hours of sudden onset right-sided hemiplegia and expressive dysphasia. His NIHSS score is 14. CT brain shows no haemorrhage and no early ischaemic changes. He has a past history of hypertension and atrial fibrillation but is not on anticoagulation. He weighs 80 kg. The stroke team has been activated and IV alteplase is planned.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 192/108 mmHg (confirmed on repeat), HR 88/min irregularly irregular, RR 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, BSL 7.2 mmol/L
data_table.Investigations: CT brain: no haemorrhage, no early ischaemic changes; INR 1.0; platelets 218 x10^9/L; creatinine 92 micromol/L

lead_in: What blood pressure management is required before alteplase administration?

options.text: No BP reduction needed as alteplase can be given at this level
Reduce BP to below 140/90 mmHg using IV sodium nitroprusside
Administer oral amlodipine 10 mg and recheck BP in 30 minutes
Defer alteplase entirely as BP above 180 mmHg is a strict exclusion
Lower BP to below 185/110 mmHg using IV glyceryl trinitrate

stem: A 44-year-old man who injects drugs presents with a 3-week history of intermittent fevers, malaise, and a new cardiac murmur. He has no history of valvular heart disease. Three sets of blood cultures drawn from separate venepuncture sites all grow Staphylococcus aureus. Transthoracic echocardiography shows a 14 mm mobile vegetation on the tricuspid valve with moderate tricuspid regurgitation. There is no aortic root abscess.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4 C, HR 98/min, BP 118/68 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air
data_table.Examination: Pansystolic murmur at left lower sternal edge increasing with inspiration, no peripheral stigmata of endocarditis, no splinter haemorrhages, no Janeway lesions, no splenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16.2 x10^9/L; CRP 148 mg/L; creatinine 82 micromol/L; 3/3 blood cultures: MSSA; TTE: 14 mm tricuspid valve vegetation, moderate TR, no abscess

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial empiric antibiotic regimen while awaiting sensitivities?

options.text: IV flucloxacillin 2 g 6-hourly for native valve MSSA
IV vancomycin 25-30 mg/kg loading then trough-guided dosing
IV benzylpenicillin 1.8 g 4-hourly with IV gentamicin
IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily with IV gentamicin 1 mg/kg dosing
IV daptomycin 8-10 mg/kg daily as a single-agent regimen

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to her GP requesting preventive therapy for migraine. She has been experiencing 6-8 migraine days per month for the past year despite optimising acute triptan use. She has a past history of hypertension well controlled on perindopril 10 mg daily, and a BMI of 32 kg/m2. She also reports low mood but is not taking antidepressants. She mentions she is keen to avoid weight gain.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 134/82 mmHg, HR 68/min, BMI 32 kg/m2
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 10 mg daily, sumatriptan 50 mg PRN (using 6-8 days per month)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line preventive medication?

options.text: Amitriptyline 10 mg nocte titrated up to 50 mg as tolerated
Candesartan 8 mg daily titrated up to 16 mg as tolerated
Sodium valproate 200 mg twice daily titrated to 500 mg BD
Propranolol 40 mg twice daily titrated to 80 mg twice daily
Topiramate 25 mg nocte titrated up to 100 mg as tolerated

stem: A 62-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset severe tearing chest pain radiating to his back. The pain began 3 hours ago and has been constant. He appears diaphoretic and in distress. There is a 22 mmHg systolic blood pressure difference between arms. Bedside echocardiography shows a dilated aortic root with an intimal flap in the ascending aorta and moderate aortic regurgitation.

data_table.Vital signs: Right arm BP 188/102 mmHg, left arm BP 166/94 mmHg, HR 108/min, RR 22/min, SpO2 95% on room air
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, early diastolic murmur at left sternal edge, equal femoral pulses, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia, LVH pattern, no acute ischaemic changes; CXR: widened mediastinum; troponin: 14 ng/L (normal below 26)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence IV sodium nitroprusside infusion for rapid BP reduction
Arrange urgent CT aortogram and defer treatment until confirmed
Commence IV esmolol infusion targeting heart rate below 60/min
Administer IV heparin bolus and prepare for emergency PCI
Administer IV hydralazine 10 mg bolus for rapid BP lowering

subtopic_detail: Preventive treatment during a cluster headache bout
stem: A 36-year-old man has had two right periorbital attacks daily for three weeks, each lasting an hour with a watering red eye. High-flow oxygen aborts them. He asks about prevention.

data_table.Attacks: Two daily for three weeks; 45 to 90 minutes each
data_table.Observations: BP 128/80, HR 72; ECG sinus rhythm, PR 160 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate preventive treatment?

options.text: Verapamil 80 mg three times daily with an ECG before each increase
Propranolol 40 mg twice daily with blood pressure review at two weeks
Amitriptyline 10 mg nightly increased to 50 mg with ECG at four weeks
Carbamazepine 100 mg twice daily with sodium checked after two weeks
Topiramate 25 mg nightly increased weekly with weight review at six weeks

stem: A 74-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden painless loss of vision in her right eye that occurred 4 hours ago. Over the past 3 weeks she has experienced new-onset right-sided temporal headaches, jaw claudication, and scalp tenderness when brushing her hair. She also reports generalised malaise and 4 kg weight loss over the same period.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6 C, HR 82/min, BP 154/86 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Right eye: visual acuity - counting fingers only, RAPD positive, pale swollen optic disc on fundoscopy; left eye: visual acuity 6/9, normal fundus; tender, thickened right temporal artery with reduced pulsation
data_table.Investigations: ESR 94 mm/hr (normal below 30); CRP 86 mg/L; platelets 462 x10^9/L; Hb 108 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily and urgent temporal artery biopsy
Urgent temporal artery biopsy before commencing any treatment
IV heparin infusion targeting APTT ratio 1.5-2.5 for the eye
Oral aspirin 300 mg and urgent ophthalmology review within 48 hours
IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days then oral taper

stem: A 58-year-old woman is reviewed in the haematology clinic 3 months after being diagnosed with a submassive pulmonary embolism. No provoking factor was identified - she had no recent surgery, immobilisation, long-haul travel, malignancy, or hormonal therapy. She completed age-appropriate cancer screening which was negative. She has been taking rivaroxaban 20 mg daily and is tolerating it well with no bleeding complications.

data_table.Investigations: CT pulmonary angiogram at 3 months: complete resolution of thrombus; D-dimer (while on anticoagulation): not performed; echocardiogram: normal RV function, no pulmonary hypertension; thrombophilia screen (off anticoagulation): negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate recommendation regarding anticoagulation duration?

options.text: Continue indefinite anticoagulation with annual bleeding review
Cease anticoagulation now as 3 months of treatment is adequate
Continue for a total of 6 months then cease and monitor
Switch to aspirin 100 mg daily as a lower-intensity alternative
Reduce to rivaroxaban 10 mg daily for extended prevention

subtopic_detail: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis
stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of fever, malaise, and a rapidly spreading painful rash. She was commenced on allopurinol 300 mg daily by her GP 3 weeks ago for gout. On examination she has widespread erythematous macules with central blistering coalescing on her trunk and limbs. Nikolsky sign is positive. The total body surface area involvement of epidermal detachment is estimated at 18%.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.8 C, HR 104/min, BP 102/66 mmHg, RR 20/min
data_table.Examination: Widespread erythematous targetoid lesions with central necrosis and sheet-like epidermal detachment over trunk, back, and proximal limbs; oral mucosal erosions; bilateral conjunctival injection with purulent discharge; genital mucosal involvement
data_table.Investigations: WCC 3.8 x10^9/L; Hb 128 g/L; platelets 142 x10^9/L; creatinine 118 micromol/L; ALT 86 U/L; albumin 28 g/L

lead_in: What is the single most important initial management step?

options.text: Commence IV ciclosporin 3 mg/kg daily as immunomodulation
Immediately cease allopurinol and arrange burns unit transfer
Commence IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days pulsed
Administer IV immunoglobulin 1 g/kg daily for 3 days total
Apply silver sulfadiazine cream to affected areas immediately

stem: A 64-year-old man with recently diagnosed advanced gastric adenocarcinoma is found to have an incidental left lower limb proximal deep vein thrombosis on staging CT. He has commenced palliative chemotherapy and has normal renal function. He has no history of GI bleeding.

data_table.Investigations: CT staging: gastric body adenocarcinoma with peritoneal metastases; incidental left common femoral and popliteal DVT; platelets 188 x10^9/L; creatinine 72 micromol/L; INR 1.0; no active upper GI bleeding on recent endoscopy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation strategy?

options.text: Warfarin with target INR 2.0-3.0 for a minimum of 6 months
Rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days then 20 mg daily
Aspirin 100 mg daily as prophylactic anticoagulation therapy
Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily
Enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg daily subcutaneously for at least 6 months

stem: A 63-year-old man presents to his GP with a 3-month history of progressive fatigue. He has no abdominal pain, no change in bowel habit, and no visible rectal bleeding. He is on no medications and has no history of GI disease. He consumes minimal alcohol. His GP orders blood tests.

data_table.Investigations: Hb 98 g/L (130-170); MCV 72 fL (80-100); ferritin 8 microg/L (30-300); transferrin saturation 8% (15-45); reticulocyte count 1.2%; B12 and folate normal; coeliac serology negative; faecal occult blood test positive

lead_in: What is the most important next investigation?

options.text: Gastroscopy and colonoscopy to exclude GI malignancy
CT abdomen and pelvis with oral and IV contrast urgently
Commence oral iron replacement and recheck haemoglobin at 8 weeks
Video capsule endoscopy to examine the entire small bowel
Repeat faecal occult blood testing on three separate samples

stem: A 28-year-old woman with BMI 38 kg/m2 presents with a 6-week history of daily generalised headaches that are worse on waking and exacerbated by coughing and straining. She also describes transient visual obscurations lasting several seconds when bending forward. She takes the oral contraceptive pill and doxycycline for acne. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral papilloedema.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/78 mmHg, HR 74/min, BMI 38 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: Bilateral papilloedema grade II, visual acuity 6/6 bilaterally, enlarged blind spots on confrontation, no focal neurological deficit, no sixth nerve palsy
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain and MRV: no mass lesion, no venous sinus thrombosis, partial empty sella, flattened posterior sclera bilaterally, distended perioptic nerve sheaths

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

options.text: Trial of acetazolamide 250 mg twice daily as empiric therapy
Lumbar puncture with opening pressure measured in lateral decubitus
CT venogram to definitively exclude cerebral venous thrombosis
Formal perimetry and optical coherence tomography of both eyes
Repeat MRI brain with fat-suppressed orbital sequences urgently

stem: A 78-year-old man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation presents to the emergency department with large-volume haematemesis and melaena. He is haemodynamically unstable. His most recent INR, taken in the ambulance, is 5.8. He weighs 70 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118/min, BP 86/52 mmHg, RR 24/min, SpO2 94% on room air
data_table.Examination: Pale, diaphoretic, tender epigastrium, melaena on PR examination
data_table.Investigations: INR 5.8; Hb 72 g/L (baseline 134); platelets 198 x10^9/L; creatinine 108 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate reversal strategy?

options.text: IV vitamin K 10 mg alone and recheck INR in 6 hours
Fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg infused over 30 minutes
Prothrombinex-VF 50 IU/kg IV with IV vitamin K 5-10 mg slowly
Oral vitamin K 5 mg and withhold warfarin for 48 hours
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV and packed red blood cells 2 units

stem: A 42-year-old non-smoking woman is diagnosed with bilateral lower lobe bronchiectasis on HRCT performed for investigation of a chronic productive cough with recurrent lower respiratory tract infections. She has had 4 courses of antibiotics in the past 12 months. She has no history of childhood pneumonia, tuberculosis, or cystic fibrosis. She reports a history of recurrent sinusitis since her twenties.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air
data_table.Investigations: HRCT chest: bilateral lower lobe cylindrical bronchiectasis with mucous plugging; sputum culture: Haemophilus influenzae; spirometry: FEV1 2.1 L (72% predicted), FVC 3.0 L, FEV1/FVC 0.70
data_table.Examination: Bibasal coarse crackles, no clubbing, no nasal polyps

lead_in: What is the most important initial investigation to identify an underlying cause?

options.text: Sweat chloride test followed by CFTR genotyping if positive
Aspergillus-specific IgE and total IgE for ABPA screening
Alpha-1 antitrypsin level and phenotyping for deficiency
Serum immunoglobulins including IgG subclasses and IgA levels
Sputum for acid-fast bacilli culture and tuberculosis PCR

stem: A 66-year-old man and current smoker presents with a 4-week history of progressive exertional dyspnoea and a dry cough. Chest X-ray shows a large right-sided pleural effusion. An ultrasound-guided diagnostic thoracentesis is performed. The pleural fluid is straw-coloured.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88/min, BP 132/82 mmHg, RR 20/min, SpO2 93% on room air
data_table.Investigations: Pleural fluid: protein 48 g/L; LDH 320 U/L; glucose 3.2 mmol/L; pH 7.28; WCC 1200 cells/microL (lymphocyte predominant). Serum: protein 68 g/L; LDH 180 U/L; albumin 32 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation for this pleural effusion?

options.text: Commence empiric IV antibiotics for a complicated parapneumonic
Therapeutic thoracentesis to relieve symptoms and then observe
Serum brain natriuretic peptide to exclude cardiac failure
Repeat thoracentesis in 2 weeks if effusion has not resolved
Pleural fluid cytology and CT chest with contrast for staging

stem: A 68-year-old post-menopausal woman is referred after a DXA scan. She has no history of fragility fractures. Her only medication is vitamin D 1000 IU daily and dietary calcium intake is adequate. She has no history of oesophageal disease, renal impairment, or malabsorption.

data_table.Investigations: DXA: T-score -2.8 lumbar spine, -2.1 femoral neck. Calcium 2.35 mmol/L (2.15-2.55). 25-OH vitamin D 68 nmol/L. eGFR 72 mL/min/1.73m2. TSH 2.1 mU/L (0.4-4.0).

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological therapy?

options.text: Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every six months
Raloxifene 60 mg orally once daily with calcium
Alendronate 70 mg orally once weekly with calcium
Zoledronic acid 5 mg intravenously once yearly
Teriparatide 20 mcg subcutaneously once daily

subtopic_detail: Lewy body dementia - recognition and initial management
stem: A 74-year-old man is brought by his wife who reports fluctuating alertness over three months, with episodes of being lucid one day and confused the next. He has vivid visual hallucinations of children in the garden that he describes in detail. His wife also notes he has become slower in his movements with a shuffling gait. He has no psychiatric history. A CT brain shows mild generalised cortical atrophy without focal lesions.

data_table.Examination: Alert but mildly confused. MMSE 21/30. Bilateral upper limb cogwheel rigidity. Mild resting tremor left hand. Shuffling gait with reduced arm swing.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TFTs, B12 - all normal. CT brain: mild generalised atrophy.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management?

options.text: Donepezil with gradual titration and regular review
Rivastigmine with cautious dose titration and review
Haloperidol low dose for hallucination management
Levodopa-carbidopa for motor symptom improvement
Memantine for moderate stage cognitive stabilisation

subtopic_detail: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy - assessment and management
stem: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 15 years presents with progressive numbness and burning pain in both feet over 6 months. He describes the pain as worse at night and rates it 7/10. He has been on metformin 2 g daily and gliclazide 160 mg daily. His most recent HbA1c was 8.2% (66 mmol/mol).

data_table.Examination: Reduced sensation to monofilament and vibration bilaterally below mid-calf. Ankle reflexes absent bilaterally. Normal power in all muscle groups. Foot pulses palpable.
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 8.2% (66 mmol/mol). B12 280 pmol/L (>150). TFTs normal. eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73m2.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological agent for his neuropathic pain?

options.text: Oxycodone 5 mg twice daily with regular review
Ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily with meals
Paracetamol 1 g four times daily with reassessment
Amitriptyline 10 mg at night with gradual titration
Carbamazepine 100 mg twice daily with dose titration

subtopic_detail: Bronchiectasis exacerbation - antibiotic selection with Pseudomonas
stem: A 57-year-old woman with known bronchiectasis presents with a 5-day history of increased sputum volume and purulence. She is febrile at 38.2 degrees Celsius with an oxygen saturation of 95% on room air. Her previous sputum cultures have grown Pseudomonas aeruginosa on two occasions in the past year. She has no penicillin allergy and her renal function is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 95% on room air, Temp 38.2 degrees C.
data_table.Investigations: FBC: WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, neutrophils 11.8 x10^9/L. CRP 68 mg/L. Sputum sent for MC&S.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric oral antibiotic?

options.text: Ciprofloxacin 750 mg orally twice daily for 14 days
Amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times daily for 14 days
Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days
Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg orally twice daily for 14 days
Azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily for 14 days

stem: A 36-year-old woman presents with a 6-week history of dry cough, bilateral ankle pain, and tender erythematous nodules on her shins. She has recently noticed blurred vision in her left eye. A chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Serum ACE is elevated at 95 U/L (8-52). A bronchoscopy with biopsy reveals non-caseating granulomata.

data_table.Investigations: CXR: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with upper lobe infiltrates. Serum ACE 95 U/L (8-52). Calcium 2.62 mmol/L (2.15-2.55). FBC, UEC, LFTs normal. Slit lamp examination: anterior uveitis left eye.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Observation with repeat chest X-ray in three months
Hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily as sole therapy
Methotrexate 10 mg weekly as steroid-sparing first-line
Inhaled budesonide with topical eye drops only
Prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg daily with ophthalmology review

subtopic_detail: Obstructive sleep apnoea - diagnosis and treatment initiation
stem: A 52-year-old man is referred by his GP for excessive daytime somnolence. His wife reports loud snoring with witnessed apnoeic episodes most nights.
