He has a BMI of 36 kg/m2, type 2 diabetes, and hypertension. His Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 14 out of 24. An in-laboratory polysomnography shows an apnoea-hypopnoea index of 32 events per hour.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 148/92 mmHg, HR 78 bpm.
data_table.Investigations: Polysomnography: AHI 32/hr, lowest SpO2 78%, arousal index 44/hr. HbA1c 7.8%. Haemoglobin 152 g/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Weight loss counselling and positional therapy only
Mandibular advancement splint with dental review
Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty referral for assessment
Nocturnal supplemental oxygen via nasal cannulae
Continuous positive airway pressure titration trial

stem: A 58-year-old man presents to your clinic concerned about a mole on his upper back that has been changing over 4 months. On examination, the lesion is an asymmetric, irregularly bordered, variably pigmented macule measuring 9 mm in diameter. There is a darkened area at the 2 o'clock position. Dermoscopy reveals an atypical pigment network, blue-white veil, and irregular dots and globules. He has a family history of melanoma in his father.

data_table.Examination: Upper back: 9 mm asymmetric, irregularly bordered macule. Variable pigmentation (brown, dark brown, black areas). Dermatoscopy: atypical pigment network, blue-white veil, irregular dots and globules. No palpable regional lymphadenopathy.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Excision biopsy with 2 mm clinical margins
Punch biopsy from the most suspicious area
Shave biopsy to determine lesion histology
Wide local excision with 10 mm clinical margins
Photographic monitoring with review in 3 months

subtopic_detail: Colorectal cancer screening - investigation of iron deficiency anaemia
stem: A 63-year-old post-menopausal woman presents with a 3-month history of increasing fatigue. She has no abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, or change in bowel habit. She has no family history of colorectal cancer. She has not participated in the National Bowel Cancer Screening Program despite receiving her kit.

data_table.Investigations: Hb 98 g/L (120-150). MCV 72 fL (80-100). Ferritin 8 mcg/L (20-200). Iron 4 micromol/L (10-30). Transferrin saturation 7% (15-45). Coeliac serology: tTG-IgA negative.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Faecal immunochemical test and dietary iron review
Oral iron replacement with repeat bloods in 8 weeks
Bidirectional endoscopy with gastroscopy and colonoscopy
CT abdomen and pelvis with oral and IV contrast
Colonoscopy alone with faecal calprotectin testing

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a firm, non-tender, 2 cm lump in the upper outer quadrant of her right breast that she noticed 3 weeks ago. It is not tethered to skin but has limited mobility. There is no nipple discharge, skin dimpling, or axillary lymphadenopathy. She has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Her last mammogram through BreastScreen was 3 years ago and was normal.

data_table.Examination: Right breast: 2 cm firm, non-tender mass at 2 o'clock position. Not fixed to skin or chest wall, limited mobility. No nipple retraction or discharge. No skin changes. No axillary lymphadenopathy bilaterally.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in investigation?

options.text: Repeat clinical examination in 6 weeks for reassessment
Mammography and targeted ultrasound with core biopsy
Breast ultrasound alone with fine needle aspiration
Breast MRI to characterise the lesion before biopsy
Excisional biopsy under general anaesthesia for diagnosis

stem: A 64-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents with progressive exertional dyspnoea over 2 years. He has a chronic productive cough. He has never had spirometry performed. He is currently taking no regular respiratory medications.

data_table.Investigations: Spirometry (post-bronchodilator): FEV1 1.42 L (predicted 3.20 L, 44% predicted). FVC 3.10 L (predicted 4.15 L, 75% predicted). FEV1/FVC ratio 0.46. Bronchodilator response: FEV1 increase 80 mL (5.6%).

lead_in: Which spirometric pattern and severity classification is correct?

options.text: Moderate obstructive defect with significant reversibility
Restrictive defect with reduced total lung capacity
Mixed obstructive and restrictive defect pattern
Severe obstructive defect with no significant reversibility
Mild obstructive defect consistent with early disease

stem: A 42-year-old man presents with chronic plaque psoriasis affecting approximately 12% of his body surface area, involving his elbows, knees, trunk, and scalp. He has been using betamethasone dipropionate ointment and calcipotriol cream for 8 months with diminishing response. He is otherwise healthy with no hepatitis B or C risk factors. His psoriasis significantly impacts his quality of life.

data_table.Investigations: FBC normal. LFTs normal. Hepatitis B surface antigen negative. Hepatitis C antibody negative. eGFR 92 mL/min/1.73m2.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in treatment?

options.text: Narrowband UVB phototherapy three times weekly
Higher potency clobetasol propionate ointment
Oral prednisolone taper over four to six weeks
Adalimumab subcutaneous injection fortnightly
Methotrexate 7.5 mg weekly with folate supplement

subtopic_detail: Ankylosing spondylitis - diagnosis and initial NSAID therapy
stem: A 28-year-old man presents with a 12-month history of progressive low back pain and stiffness that is worst in the morning, lasting 90 minutes, and improves with activity. He wakes at night with pain and finds that exercise helps. He has a history of anterior uveitis in his left eye 6 months ago. His father has ankylosing spondylitis. NSAIDs have not been trialled.

data_table.Examination: Reduced lumbar flexion. Positive modified Schober test (expansion <4 cm). Reduced chest expansion (2.5 cm). Bilateral sacroiliac joint tenderness.
data_table.Investigations: CRP 28 mg/L (<5). ESR 32 mm/hr (<20). HLA-B27 positive. Pelvic X-ray: bilateral sacroiliitis grade 2.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological therapy?

options.text: Methotrexate 15 mg weekly with folate supplementation
Adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneously fortnightly
Sulfasalazine 1 g twice daily with dose titration
Prednisolone 25 mg daily with gastric protection
Naproxen 500 mg twice daily with gastroprotection

stem: A 48-year-old man of Northern European ancestry presents with fatigue and arthralgia in his second and third metacarpophalangeal joints bilaterally. He consumes 2-3 standard drinks on weekends. His GP ordered iron studies which showed markedly elevated transferrin saturation and ferritin.

data_table.Investigations: Fasting transferrin saturation 72% (15-45). Ferritin 1450 mcg/L (30-300). ALT 58 U/L (<40). AST 52 U/L (<35). FBC normal. eGFR 88 mL/min/1.73m2. Fasting glucose 6.8 mmol/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Liver biopsy with Perls Prussian blue staining
HFE gene testing for C282Y and H63D mutations
MRI liver with T2-star mapping for iron content
Repeat fasting iron studies in 4 weeks for confirmation
Abdominal ultrasound with hepatic elastography

subtopic_detail: Adult cardiac arrest - ALS drug timing in shockable rhythm
stem: You are leading a resuscitation for a 55-year-old man who collapsed in the emergency department with witnessed ventricular fibrillation. High-quality CPR was commenced immediately. Two defibrillation shocks have been delivered at 200 J each without return of spontaneous circulation. The rhythm remains ventricular fibrillation.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Amiodarone 300 mg IV bolus after the next shock
Lidocaine 100 mg IV bolus as antiarrhythmic
Adrenaline 1 mg IV bolus with ongoing CPR
Atropine 3 mg IV bolus for vagal tone
Magnesium sulfate 5 mmol IV over 2 minutes

subtopic_detail: Shock classification - distributive vs cardiogenic discrimination
stem: A 72-year-old man presents to the emergency department with hypotension. He was found by ambulance with altered consciousness. He has a background of ischaemic heart disease with previous anterior STEMI 3 years ago and chronic heart failure. He has also been feeling unwell with fevers for 2 days. His family reports recent urinary symptoms.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 112 bpm, BP 78/42 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 92% on room air, Temp 39.1 degrees C.
data_table.Examination: Warm peripheries. Bounding pulses. JVP not elevated. Chest: bibasal crackles. Abdomen: suprapubic tenderness. Urine dipstick: leucocytes +++, nitrites positive.
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 5.8 mmol/L. WCC 18.4 x10^9/L. CRP 186 mg/L. Troponin <5 ng/L. NT-proBNP 620 pg/mL (baseline 480). ECG: sinus tachycardia, old Q waves anterior leads.

lead_in: What is the most likely type of shock?

options.text: Cardiogenic shock from acute heart failure exacerbation
Hypovolaemic shock from inadequate fluid intake
Obstructive shock from massive pulmonary embolism
Mixed cardiogenic and hypovolaemic shock pattern
Distributive shock from urosepsis with warm peripheries

subtopic_detail: Acute viral myocarditis - recognition and initial management
stem: A 26-year-old man presents with central chest pain that has been worsening over 24 hours. He had a coryzal illness 10 days ago. The pain is sharp, pleuritic, and partially relieved by sitting forward. He has no cardiovascular risk factors and no family history of sudden cardiac death.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, Temp 37.8 degrees C.
data_table.Investigations: ECG: diffuse ST elevation in leads I, II, aVF, V3-V6 with PR depression. Troponin I 2800 ng/L (<26). NT-proBNP 340 pg/mL (<125). CRP 48 mg/L. FBC normal. Coronary angiography: normal coronary arteries.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: CT coronary angiography with calcium scoring
Repeat troponin and ECG in 6 hours for trending
Endomyocardial biopsy under fluoroscopic guidance
Cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement
Transthoracic echocardiography with strain imaging

stem: A 44-year-old woman presents with widespread body pain for over 12 months affecting her neck, shoulders, back, and both legs. She also reports significant fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, and cognitive difficulties she describes as 'brain fog'. She has seen multiple specialists without a diagnosis. She has no joint swelling or morning stiffness lasting beyond 15 minutes. She has tried paracetamol with minimal benefit.

data_table.Examination: Multiple tender points at bilateral trapezius, lateral epicondyles, greater trochanters, and medial fat pads of knees. No joint synovitis, swelling, or effusion. Full range of movement at all joints. Neurological examination normal.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, CRP, ESR, TFTs, ANA, RF, anti-CCP - all normal. HbA1c 5.2%.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management approach?

options.text: Tramadol 50 mg four times daily for pain control
Prednisolone 15 mg daily for a 4-week therapeutic trial
Naproxen 500 mg twice daily with gastroprotection
Referral to a rheumatologist for further investigation
Graduated exercise program with amitriptyline at night

subtopic_detail: Denosumab cessation - rebound vertebral fracture risk
stem: A 72-year-old woman has been on denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months for 5 years for osteoporosis, with good response. She wishes to cease treatment due to needle anxiety. Her most recent DXA shows T-score -1.8 at the lumbar spine, improved from -3.2 at initiation. She has no history of fragility fractures. Her eGFR is 52 mL/min/1.73m2.

data_table.Investigations: DXA: T-score -1.8 lumbar spine, -1.5 femoral neck. Calcium 2.38 mmol/L. 25-OH vitamin D 72 nmol/L. eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73m2.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management strategy?

options.text: Transition to oral alendronate before ceasing denosumab
Cease denosumab immediately given improved bone density
Continue denosumab indefinitely as cessation is unsafe
Transition to zoledronic acid given her renal impairment
Taper denosumab to annual dosing over the next 2 years

stem: A 58-year-old woman presents with 3 months of fatigue, polyuria, and constipation. She has a history of recurrent nephrolithiasis. She takes no calcium supplements or vitamin D. She has no known malignancy. There is no family history of endocrine disorders.

data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.92 mmol/L (2.15-2.55). Phosphate 0.68 mmol/L (0.80-1.50). PTH 12.8 pmol/L (1.6-6.9). 25-OH vitamin D 48 nmol/L. eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73m2. 24-hour urinary calcium 9.2 mmol/day (2.5-7.5).

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy from PTHrP
Vitamin D intoxication from excess supplementation
Primary hyperparathyroidism from parathyroid adenoma
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia from CaSR mutation
Granulomatous disease with extrarenal calcitriol production

stem: A 32-year-old woman on risperidone 4 mg daily for schizophrenia presents with galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea for 6 months. She is sexually active and a pregnancy test is negative. Her psychiatrist requests a prolactin level, which returns markedly elevated. Previous prolactin levels before starting risperidone were not available.

data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 4200 mU/L (<500). TSH 2.1 mU/L (0.4-4.0). Beta-hCG negative. LH 1.2 IU/L. FSH 2.4 IU/L. Renal function normal.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease risperidone and recheck prolactin in 6 weeks
MRI pituitary with gadolinium contrast enhancement
Switch to aripiprazole which lowers prolactin levels
Measure macroprolactin to exclude laboratory artefact
Add cabergoline 0.25 mg weekly to reduce prolactin

stem: A 46-year-old man is referred with increasing ring and shoe size over 3 years. He reports headaches, excessive sweating, and joint pain. He was recently diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. His dentist noted widening interdental spaces. On examination he has coarse facial features, macroglossia, and doughy hands.

data_table.Investigations: IGF-1 68 nmol/L (12-38 for age and sex). Random GH 8.2 mcg/L. HbA1c 7.4%. Visual fields full to confrontation. Fasting glucose 8.2 mmol/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: 24-hour GH sampling with mean level calculation
MRI pituitary with gadolinium as the definitive test
Repeat IGF-1 in 4 weeks to confirm persistent elevation
Insulin tolerance test to assess GH reserve dynamics
Oral glucose tolerance test with GH suppression profile

stem: A 58-year-old man is brought by his wife who reports progressive personality change over 18 months. He has become disinhibited, making inappropriate sexual comments to strangers, and recently shoplifted despite no financial difficulty. He has developed a compulsive fixation on eating sweet foods and has gained 12 kg. He shows no concern about his behaviour and lacks insight. His memory for recent events remains relatively intact. His father had a progressive neurological condition diagnosed in his 50s.

data_table.Examination: MMSE 26/30 (lost points for attention and visuospatial). Primitive reflexes present bilaterally (grasp reflex, palmomental). No parkinsonism. No motor neurone signs. Speech fluent but tangential.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TFTs, B12 - normal. MRI brain: bilateral frontal and anterior temporal lobe atrophy, greater on the right. No vascular changes.

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Late-onset bipolar disorder with manic features
Early-onset Alzheimer disease with behavioural variant
Dementia with Lewy bodies presenting with disinhibition
Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia
Vascular dementia from subcortical ischaemic disease

subtopic_detail: Motor neurone disease - clinical recognition and differentiation
stem: A 62-year-old man presents with progressive difficulty gripping objects with his right hand over 8 months. He has noticed fasciculations in his forearms and thighs. He has developed slurred speech in the past 2 months. He denies sensory symptoms, bowel or bladder dysfunction, or neck pain. MRI cervical spine performed by his GP was normal.

data_table.Examination: Wasting and fasciculations of right thenar eminence and first dorsal interosseous. Brisk reflexes in all four limbs including jaw jerk. Bilateral extensor plantar responses. Tongue fasciculations with mild wasting. Sensation intact throughout. Cerebellar examination normal.
data_table.Investigations: MRI cervical spine: no cord compression or myelopathy signal. FBC, UEC, LFTs, TFTs, CRP, glucose - normal. CK mildly elevated at 380 U/L (<220).

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with bulbar involvement
Cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy
Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block
Kennedy disease with X-linked bulbospinal atrophy
Myasthenia gravis with progressive generalised weakness

subtopic_detail: DRESS syndrome - recognition and discrimination from SJS/TEN
stem: A 54-year-old man presents with a widespread morbilliform rash, facial oedema, and fever 5 weeks after starting allopurinol 300 mg daily for gout. He has cervical lymphadenopathy. He reports no mucosal ulceration or skin blistering.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102 bpm, BP 132/78 mmHg, Temp 38.8 degrees C.
data_table.Investigations: FBC: WCC 14.8 x10^9/L with eosinophils 3.2 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5). ALT 286 U/L (<40). AST 198 U/L (<35). ALP 142 U/L (30-110). Bilirubin 22 micromol/L (<20). Creatinine 138 micromol/L (60-110). CRP 86 mg/L.

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Stevens-Johnson syndrome from allopurinol exposure
Viral exanthem with coincidental liver derangement
Acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis from allopurinol
Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms
Serum sickness-like reaction to xanthine oxidase inhibitor

subtopic_detail: Incidental pulmonary nodule - risk assessment and surveillance
stem: A 62-year-old man with a 30-pack-year smoking history has a CT chest performed for investigation of rib pain after a fall. A solitary solid pulmonary nodule measuring 7 mm is incidentally found in the right upper lobe. There is no mediastinal lymphadenopathy. He has no previous CT imaging for comparison. He has no history of malignancy and no constitutional symptoms.

data_table.Investigations: CT chest: 7 mm solid nodule right upper lobe, smooth borders, no calcification. No mediastinal lymphadenopathy. No pleural effusion. Rib fractures 9th and 10th right.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of the incidental pulmonary nodule?

options.text: Immediate CT-guided biopsy for tissue diagnosis
Follow-up CT chest at 6-12 months and then annually
PET-CT scan for metabolic characterisation of nodule
No follow-up needed as nodule is below the size threshold
Referral for video-assisted thoracoscopic resection

subtopic_detail: Elevated PSA - interpretation and further investigation
stem: A 64-year-old man presents after a routine health check revealed a PSA of 6.8 mcg/L. He has no urinary symptoms, no family history of prostate cancer, and no previous PSA testing. Digital rectal examination performed by his GP was normal. He takes finasteride 5 mg daily for male pattern hair loss.

data_table.Investigations: PSA 6.8 mcg/L (age-adjusted reference <4.5 for 60-69). Free-to-total PSA ratio 12%. Previous PSA: none available. DRE: smooth, non-tender prostate, no nodules.

lead_in: What is the most important consideration when interpreting this PSA result?

The normal DRE excludes clinically significant cancer
Finasteride halves PSA so the true level is approximately double
The low free-to-total ratio suggests benign prostatic cause
Age-adjusted reference range makes this result acceptable

subtopic_detail: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis vs hypersensitivity pneumonitis - discrimination
stem: A 68-year-old retired farmer presents with progressive exertional dyspnoea and dry cough over 18 months. He is a lifelong non-smoker. He kept racing pigeons for 25 years until 5 years ago. data_table.Investigations: Spirometry: FVC 62% predicted, FEV1/FVC ratio 0.84. DLCO 48% predicted. options.text: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis with UIP pattern
Non-specific interstitial pneumonia from unknown cause
Sarcoidosis with pulmonary fibrosis progression
Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis from avian antigens
Asbestosis from occupational farming exposure history

subtopic_detail: Chronic hepatitis B - treatment indication assessment
stem: A 38-year-old man born in Vietnam is found to be hepatitis B surface antigen positive on routine screening. He is asymptomatic. He was diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B 5 years ago in Vietnam but never commenced treatment. He has no other medical conditions and takes no regular medications.

data_table.Investigations: HBsAg positive. HBeAg negative. Anti-HBe positive. HBV DNA 28,000 IU/mL. ALT 78 U/L (<40) - persistently elevated on 3 occasions over 6 months. AST 62 U/L. Platelet count 168 x10^9/L. FibroScan: 8.2 kPa (F2 fibrosis). AFP 4.2 mcg/L (<10). Hepatitis D antibody negative.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

Pegylated interferon alfa-2a for 48 weeks as first-line
Lamivudine 100 mg daily as initial antiviral therapy
Liver biopsy for histological grading before treatment
Entecavir 0.5 mg daily as long-term antiviral therapy

subtopic_detail: Severe alcohol-related hepatitis - Maddrey discriminant function and prednisolone
stem: A 48-year-old man with a history of heavy alcohol consumption (>80 g/day for 20 years) presents with 2 weeks of progressive jaundice, right upper quadrant tenderness, and fever. He last consumed alcohol 3 days ago. He has no evidence of GI bleeding or encephalopathy. An abdominal ultrasound shows hepatomegaly with no biliary obstruction.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96 bpm, BP 108/68 mmHg, Temp 38.2 degrees C.
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 182 micromol/L (<20). ALT 88 U/L (<40). AST 196 U/L (<35). ALP 168 U/L (30-110). INR 2.1. Albumin 26 g/L (35-50). WCC 14.6 x10^9/L. Platelet 98 x10^9/L. Creatinine 92 micromol/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Prednisolone 40 mg daily for 28 days with Lille assessment
N-acetylcysteine infusion alone without corticosteroids
Pentoxifylline 400 mg three times daily for 28 days

Supportive care only with nutritional supplementation

subtopic_detail: Pituitary apoplexy - recognition and emergency management
stem: A 50-year-old man with a known 18 mm pituitary macroadenoma (non-functioning) under surveillance presents to the emergency department with sudden severe thunderclap headache, vomiting, and acute visual deterioration over 4 hours. He reports he can no longer see objects in his right visual field with either eye. He was commenced on anticoagulation with apixaban 3 weeks ago for a new diagnosis of atrial fibrillation.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 52 bpm, BP 88/54 mmHg, Temp 36.2 degrees C.
data_table.Examination: GCS 14 (E3V5M6). Right homonymous hemianopia on confrontation. Left partial third nerve palsy with ptosis. Meningism present.
data_table.Investigations: CT head: haemorrhagic pituitary mass with suprasellar extension. Sodium 128 mmol/L. Cortisol 42 nmol/L (morning reference 150-600). TSH 0.3 mU/L. Free T4 8.2 pmol/L (10-20).

lead_in: What is the most critical immediate intervention?

options.text: Urgent MRI pituitary before any treatment decision
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat and fluid resuscitation
Emergency neurosurgical decompression within 6 hours
Levothyroxine 100 mcg daily for secondary hypothyroidism
Reversal of apixaban with andexanet alfa infusion

subtopic_detail: Beta-thalassaemia trait vs iron deficiency - discrimination
stem: A 28-year-old woman of Mediterranean ancestry presents for a routine antenatal visit at 12 weeks gestation. Her GP noted microcytic anaemia on her initial bloods. She has no symptoms of anaemia and reports a normal diet. She has had mild microcytic anaemia documented on previous blood tests but was never investigated further.

data_table.Investigations: Hb 108 g/L (115-160). MCV 64 fL (80-100). MCH 22 pg (27-32). RCC 5.8 x10^12/L (3.8-5.2). RDW 13.5% (<14.5). Ferritin 68 mcg/L (20-200). Iron 14 micromol/L (10-30). Transferrin saturation 28% (15-45).

lead_in: What is the most likely cause of her microcytic anaemia?

options.text: Iron deficiency anaemia from dietary insufficiency
Anaemia of chronic disease from pregnancy physiology
Beta-thalassaemia trait with characteristic red cell indices
Sideroblastic anaemia from pyridoxine deficiency
Alpha-thalassaemia with two-gene deletion carrier state

subtopic_detail: Post-cardiac arrest - targeted temperature management and neuroprognostication
stem: A 58-year-old man achieves return of spontaneous circulation after 22 minutes of CPR for witnessed ventricular fibrillation in a shopping centre. He remains comatose (GCS 3T) on arrival to the emergency department. He is intubated and ventilated. His initial ECG post-ROSC shows sinus tachycardia with no ST elevation. A CT brain is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108 bpm, BP 92/58 mmHg (on noradrenaline 0.1 mcg/kg/min), SpO2 96% on FiO2 0.5.
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 8.4 mmol/L. pH 7.18. Potassium 3.8 mmol/L. Glucose 12.4 mmol/L. Troponin 420 ng/L. CT brain: no acute intracranial pathology.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate targeted temperature management strategy?

options.text: Therapeutic hypothermia at 33 degrees C for 24 hours
Cool to 36 degrees C for 24 hours per TTM1 protocol
No active temperature management needed in this case
Targeted normothermia at 37.5 degrees C with active fever prevention
Rapid cooling to 32 degrees C within 4 hours of ROSC

subtopic_detail: RA vs PsA vs reactive vs gout - pattern recognition
stem: A 38-year-old man presents to a HNE LHD rheumatology clinic with 8 weeks of asymmetric joint pain affecting the right second and third distal interphalangeal joints, left knee and left Achilles insertion. He has a 4-year history of scalp scaling treated with topical betamethasone. There is dactylitis of the left third toe. C-reactive protein (CRP) 28 mg/L, rheumatoid factor negative, anti-CCP negative, uric acid 0.36 mmol/L. Hand X-ray: bone proliferation and central erosion at the right second DIP joint with periostitis.

data_table.Serology: RF negative, anti-CCP negative, ANA negative, HLA-B27 not done.
data_table.Imaging: DIP central erosion with bone proliferation, periostitis.

lead_in: Which feature best discriminates the most likely diagnosis from the leading alternatives?

options.text: Dactylitis with DIP involvement and bone proliferation on imaging
Negative rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies
Asymmetric joint distribution affecting fewer than five joints
Serum urate level of 0.36 mmol/L within reference range
Personal history of scalp scaling treated with topical steroid

subtopic_detail: DMARD escalation and biologic switch - infection screening
stem: A 54-year-old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis has persistent DAS28 of 5.2 after 6 months of methotrexate 25 mg weekly plus sulfasalazine 1 g twice daily plus hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily. Her rheumatologist proposes adding a tumour necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitor. She was born in Vietnam, migrated to Australia aged 22, and had a positive Mantoux test 10 years ago after a household contact; chest X-ray then was normal and she received no treatment.

data_table.Disease: Seropositive RA, DAS28 5.2 after triple csDMARD 6/12.
data_table.TB risk: Vietnam birth, positive Mantoux 10 years ago, CXR normal then, no treatment.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step before starting the TNF inhibitor?

options.text: Interferon-gamma release assay plus hepatitis B and C serology
Start the TNF inhibitor and monitor for tuberculosis symptoms monthly
Repeat the Mantoux test and proceed if induration less than 5 mm
Switch to a JAK inhibitor instead of a TNF inhibitor to avoid screening
Order chest computed tomography and proceed if no active lesions

subtopic_detail: GCA + PMR overlap - temporal artery biopsy decision
stem: A 74-year-old woman presents to a Central Coast LHD emergency department with 5 days of right-sided headache, jaw pain after chewing for several minutes, and 6 weeks of bilateral shoulder and hip girdle stiffness lasting 2 hours each morning. Vision is normal. The right superficial temporal artery is tender and non-pulsatile. CRP 96 mg/L, ESR 88 mm/h, haemoglobin 105 g/L (normocytic), platelets 462. The on-call team gives prednisolone 60 mg orally and arranges temporal artery biopsy for 4 days' time.

data_table.Symptoms: Headache, jaw claudication, PMR-pattern girdle stiffness, no visual loss.
data_table.Examination: Right temporal artery tender, non-pulsatile.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate position on the temporal artery biopsy timing?

options.text: Biopsy within 2 weeks of starting steroids remains diagnostic in most cases
Steroids should be withheld until after biopsy to preserve diagnostic yield
Temporal artery ultrasound replaces biopsy in all Australian centres
Biopsy is unnecessary given the classic clinical picture and elevated inflammatory markers
Biopsy after 4 days of steroid therapy is non-diagnostic and should be cancelled

stem: A 62-year-old man is admitted to a HNE LHD renal unit with 3 weeks of fatigue, weight loss, haemoptysis and rising creatinine. Investigations: creatinine 312 micromol/L (baseline 92), urinalysis 3+ blood 2+ protein with dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts. ANCA: PR3-ANCA positive at high titre. Chest CT: bilateral cavitating pulmonary nodules. Renal biopsy: pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis with 60% crescents. He is dialysis-independent and has no alveolar haemorrhage. He has a 15-year remote history of bladder cancer in remission.

data_table.Renal: Cr 312 (baseline 92), active urinary sediment, 60% crescents on biopsy.
data_table.Severity: Organ-threatening (kidney, lung) but not life-threatening (no DAH, dialysis-independent).

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate induction regimen?

Plasma exchange plus oral prednisolone alone
Methotrexate 25 mg weekly plus oral prednisolone
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day as monotherapy

stem: A 34-year-old woman is referred to a HNE LHD haematology clinic after a second unprovoked deep vein thrombosis. She had a first DVT aged 30 and one previous late pregnancy loss. Antiphospholipid antibody screen: lupus anticoagulant positive on two occasions 14 weeks apart, anti-cardiolipin IgG 78 GPL units (high titre), anti-beta2-glycoprotein-1 IgG positive. Renal function and full blood count are normal. She asks whether she can switch from warfarin to apixaban for convenience.

data_table.Diagnosis: Triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), recurrent venous events.
data_table.Antibody profile: LA positive x2, aCL IgG high titre, anti-beta2-GP1 IgG positive.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Continue warfarin; direct oral anticoagulants increase thrombotic events in triple-positive APS
Switch to apixaban 5 mg twice daily; equivalent efficacy in all APS subgroups
Switch to rivaroxaban 20 mg daily; warfarin INR monitoring is unnecessary
Switch to low molecular weight heparin long-term to avoid INR monitoring
Stop anticoagulation; two unprovoked venous events do not justify lifelong therapy

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulation choice in valvular AF and severe renal impairment
stem: A 72-year-old man with moderate mitral stenosis (rheumatic) and new persistent atrial fibrillation is reviewed at a Central Coast LHD cardiology clinic. CHA2DS2-VA score 4. Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) 28 mL/min/1.73 m2 (CKD stage 4). No prior bleeding. He has heard about apixaban from a friend and asks for it instead of warfarin.

Rivaroxaban 15 mg daily reduced for renal impairment
Aspirin 100 mg daily as monotherapy

subtopic_detail: Extended VTE therapy - decision at 3 months
stem: A 48-year-old man completed 3 months of apixaban for an unprovoked proximal deep vein thrombosis. He has no thrombophilia (negative full panel), no malignancy on age-appropriate screening, normal D-dimer 4 weeks after stopping anticoagulation would be needed for HERDOO2-style assessment in women but he is male. Switch to aspirin 100 mg daily as extended secondary prevention

subtopic_detail: ITP vs TTP vs HUS - adult distinction
stem: A 36-year-old woman is admitted to a HNE LHD emergency department with 3 days of confusion, fever and bruising. Vital signs: temperature 38.4, heart rate 112, blood pressure 138/86. Examination: petechiae over lower limbs, no splenomegaly, fluctuating confusion. data_table.Pentad features: Fever, neuro changes, AKI, thrombocytopenia, MAHA.
data_table.Bloods: Hb 78, Plt 14, retics up, bilirubin 48, LDH 1240, haptoglobin undetectable.

options.text: Urgent plasma exchange plus corticosteroid, before ADAMTS13 result

Intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg plus oral prednisolone
Empirical ceftriaxone plus supportive care pending blood cultures

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to a Central Coast LHD general practice with 3 months of fatigue. She has heavy menstrual periods and follows a vegetarian diet. Full blood count: haemoglobin 92 g/L, mean cell volume (MCV) 68 fL, mean cell haemoglobin 22 pg, red cell distribution width raised. White cells and platelets normal. Normal ferritin, normal transferrin saturation, normal MCV

stem: A 67-year-old woman presents to a HNE LHD general practice with 4 months of fatigue, paraesthesia in both feet and an unsteady gait. Full blood count: haemoglobin 96 g/L, MCV 116 fL, white cells 4.2, platelets 130. Blood film: oval macrocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils. LDH raised, indirect bilirubin mildly raised. data_table.Haemolysis markers: LDH up, indirect bilirubin mildly up.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Serum vitamin B12 and red cell folate levels

subtopic_detail: Anaemia in CKD - ESA initiation threshold
stem: A 68-year-old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease (eGFR 22) is reviewed at a HNE LHD renal clinic. Haemoglobin 92 g/L, MCV 88 fL. Iron studies: ferritin 180 microg/L, transferrin saturation 28%. Vitamin B12 and folate normal. Faecal occult blood negative. No bleeding. He reports fatigue limiting daily walks.

stem: A 22-year-old woman with homozygous sickle cell disease presents to a HNE LHD emergency department with 24 hours of right upper-quadrant and back pain typical of her vaso-occlusive crises, treated with intravenous opioid analgesia. Six hours later she becomes dyspnoeic with new fever 38.6, oxygen saturation 88% room air, respiratory rate 28, and chest X-ray shows new bilateral lower lobe infiltrates. Haemoglobin 68 g/L (baseline 82), platelets 320, white cells 18.

data_table.Disease: Homozygous sickle cell, in vaso-occlusive crisis 24 h.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

subtopic_detail: Crystal vs septic arthritis - joint aspiration
stem: A 56-year-old man presents to a Central Coast LHD emergency department with 8 hours of severe right knee pain, swelling and erythema. Temperature 37.4, heart rate 96. data_table.Joint: Right knee, hot swollen erythematous, 8 h.

lead_in: Which synovial fluid finding most strongly supports a gout flare over septic arthritis?

stem: A 28-year-old man presents to a HNE LHD general practice with 3 weeks of asymmetric oligoarthritis affecting the left knee and right ankle, with bilateral Achilles enthesitis. He recalls a 5-day diarrhoeal illness with bloody stools 3 weeks before joint symptoms began, while travelling regionally. He also has conjunctivitis and sterile dysuria. CRP 56 mg/L, RF negative, anti-CCP negative, urate 0.32 mmol/L. Stool culture from the diarrhoeal episode grew Campylobacter jejuni. HIV testing negative.

data_table.Preceding: Bloody diarrhoea 3 weeks earlier, Campylobacter jejuni isolated.
data_table.Serology: RF neg, anti-CCP neg, urate normal, HIV neg.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Naproxen 500 mg twice daily with proton pump inhibitor cover and review at 4 weeks

stem:
A 38-year-old man was diagnosed with HIV two months ago with a CD4 count of 42 cells per microlitre and a viral load of 320,000 copies per mL. He was commenced on tenofovir, emtricitabine, and dolutegravir. At his 6-week review, his viral load has fallen to 800 copies per mL and CD4 has risen to 145 cells per microlitre. data_table.Vital signs: HR 92 bpm, BP 132/84 mmHg, T 38.4 C, GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6).
data_table.Investigations: CD4 145 cells per microlitre (baseline 42), viral load 800 copies per mL (baseline 320,000), WCC 8.4 x10^9/L, CRP 68 mg/L. Serum toxoplasma IgG positive. CSF opening pressure 22 cmH2O, protein 0.82 g/L, glucose 3.1 mmol/L (serum 5.8).

subtopic_detail: Advice about infectivity and work after a diagnosis of latent infection
stem: A 34-year-old childcare worker has a positive interferon gamma release assay from routine screening. She is asymptomatic, active disease has been excluded, and she is about to start preventive treatment. She asks about work and her family.

data_table.Examination: Well, afebrile, chest clear, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Interferon gamma release assay positive; chest radiograph normal; HIV negative

lead_in: What advice is most appropriate?

options.text: She is not infectious and may continue working
She must stay off work until treatment finishes
Her household contacts need screening for infection

She should wear a mask at work for two weeks

stem: A 45-year-old woman originally from Ethiopia, living in Australia for 2 years, presents with 3 months of progressive abdominal distension, 6 kg weight loss, drenching night sweats, and low-grade fevers. She has no respiratory symptoms and her chest X-ray is normal. Abdominal examination reveals shifting dullness consistent with ascites. CT abdomen shows moderate ascites, diffuse peritoneal thickening and enhancement, and mesenteric lymphadenopathy with central necrosis. Serum CA-125 is elevated at 280 U/mL. A diagnostic paracentesis yields straw-coloured fluid with a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 6 g/L.

data_table.Investigations: Ascitic fluid: protein 52 g/L, SAAG 6 g/L, WCC 840 cells per microlitre (90% lymphocytes), glucose 2.8 mmol/L, LDH 320 U/L, ADA 78 U/L (normal < 30). Cytology: reactive mesothelial cells, no malignant cells. CA-125: 280 U/mL. IGRA: positive. Hb 106 g/L, ESR 68 mm/hr, CRP 42 mg/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

options.text: Laparoscopic peritoneal biopsy for histology and mycobacterial culture
Three early-morning sputum samples for AFB smear microscopy and TB culture
Empirical anti-tuberculosis therapy without tissue diagnosis based on clinical picture
CT-guided fine needle aspiration of necrotic mesenteric lymph node for culture
Repeat diagnostic paracentesis with larger volume for improved culture sensitivity

stem: A 68-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and COPD presents to the emergency department with 2 days of productive cough, fever, and rigors. She takes metformin, tiotropium, and salbutamol. On arrival she is drowsy but rousable, with temperature 39.2 degrees C, heart rate 112 bpm, respiratory rate 28, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg, and SpO2 91% on room air. A venous blood gas shows lactate 4.2 mmol/L. Blood cultures and a chest X-ray showing right lower lobe consolidation have been obtained. Two large-bore cannulae have been placed.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.2 C, HR 112 bpm, RR 28, BP 88/52 mmHg, SpO2 91% room air, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6).
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.28, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, HCO3 18 mmol/L. CXR: right lower lobe consolidation. WCC 18.6 x10^9/L, CRP 312 mg/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 78).

lead_in: What is the single most important intervention to deliver within the next 60 minutes?

options.text: Commence a noradrenaline infusion to target a MAP above 65 mmHg urgently
Administer IV broad-spectrum antibiotics appropriate for the suspected source
Perform urgent CT pulmonary angiogram to exclude concomitant pulmonary embolism
Insert a central venous catheter for central venous pressure-guided resuscitation
Administer IV hydrocortisone 200 mg daily for suspected adrenal insufficiency

subtopic_detail: Refractory septic shock vasopressor and adjunctive therapy
stem:
A 62-year-old man with perforated sigmoid diverticulitis is in the ICU following emergency laparotomy and Hartmann's procedure 6 hours ago. Despite source control surgery, he has received 40 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid and noradrenaline has been titrated to 0.4 mcg/kg/min. His MAP remains 56 mmHg. He has been on appropriate broad-spectrum antibiotics (IV piperacillin-tazobactam and IV metronidazole) since the emergency department.

A repeat lactate is 5.8 mmol/L (was 4.1 pre-operatively). Bedside echocardiography shows hyperdynamic left ventricular function with a small, underfilled IVC showing greater than 50% respiratory variation.

data_table.Vital signs: MAP 56 mmHg on noradrenaline 0.4 mcg/kg/min, HR 118 bpm, T 38.8 C, SpO2 94% on 6 L nasal prongs.
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 5.8 mmol/L (was 4.1), pH 7.24, WCC 22.4 x10^9/L, CRP 380 mg/L, creatinine 188 micromol/L, Hb 92 g/L, platelets 86 x10^9/L. Echo: hyperdynamic LV, small IVC with > 50% respiratory variation.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step to manage the refractory shock?

options.text: Increase noradrenaline infusion rate to 1.0 mcg per kg per min as monotherapy
Commence dobutamine 5 mcg per kg per min for inotropic cardiac support now
Switch to IV adrenaline infusion and cease noradrenaline infusion immediately
Administer IV albumin 4% at 20 mL per kg for volume expansion and MAP support
Add IV vasopressin 0.03 units per min and commence IV hydrocortisone 50 mg QID

stem: A 35-year-old previously healthy woman presents with 3 days of fever, headache, and behavioural change. Her partner reports she has been increasingly confused, with word-finding difficulties and episodes of agitation. Today she had a witnessed 90-second tonic-clonic seizure at home. On examination she is febrile, disoriented to time and place, and has a receptive aphasia. There is no rash and no nuchal rigidity. MRI brain shows T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and swelling in the left temporal lobe extending to the insular cortex. CSF shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 C, HR 98 bpm, BP 134/82 mmHg, GCS 12 (E3 V3 M6).
data_table.Investigations: MRI: T2/FLAIR hyperintensity left temporal lobe and insula with mild mass effect. CSF: WCC 86 cells per microlitre (95% lymphocytes), protein 0.92 g/L, glucose 3.4 mmol/L (serum 5.2), RBC 120 per microlitre. CSF HSV PCR: pending (result expected in 24-48 hours).

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Await CSF HSV PCR result before starting treatment to confirm the diagnosis
IV ceftriaxone 2 g twelve-hourly with dexamethasone for bacterial meningitis cover
IV aciclovir 10 mg per kg eight-hourly immediately plus levetiracetam for seizures
Oral valaciclovir 1 g three times daily as equivalent to intravenous aciclovir
IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days for suspected autoimmune encephalitis

subtopic_detail: Necrotising fasciitis recognition and urgent management
stem:
A 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and obesity presents with a 3-day history of rapidly spreading redness, swelling, and severe pain in his left lower leg following a minor skin abrasion. He has been on oral flucloxacillin from his GP for 48 hours without improvement. On examination, the erythema has extended 8 cm beyond the pen markings placed yesterday.

The skin is dusky with two haemorrhagic bullae. He describes the pain as out of proportion to the visible changes. Crepitus is palpable over the medial calf.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.1 C, HR 122 bpm, BP 92/58 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 96%.
data_table.Investigations: WCC 24.8 x10^9/L, CRP 342 mg/L, Na 131 mmol/L, creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 88), glucose 18.4 mmol/L, Hb 108 g/L, lactate 3.8 mmol/L. X-ray left leg: subcutaneous gas.

lead_in: What is the most important next step in management?

options.text: Switch oral flucloxacillin to IV flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours and observe
Urgent surgical debridement with IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and resuscitation
Urgent MRI of the left leg to confirm fascial involvement before any surgery
Incision and drainage at the bedside as this is likely a deep soft tissue abscess
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy as the primary treatment with antibiotics as adjunct

stem: A 55-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance with a 12-hour history of worsening headache, photophobia, and confusion. She has no significant past medical history and takes no regular medications. On examination she has neck stiffness and a positive Kernig sign. There is no rash. A CT brain performed urgently shows no mass lesion or hydrocephalus.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 145/88 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 97% RA, Temp 39.6, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6)
data_table.Investigations: FBC: WCC 19.4 x10^9/L; CRP 210 mg/L; UEC normal; coagulation studies normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric treatment?

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 2 g BD and IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading
IV benzylpenicillin 1.8 g 4-hourly as monotherapy for cover
IV ampicillin 2 g 4-hourly and IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily
IV fluconazole 400 mg daily with a lumbar puncture for culture
IV dexamethasone, then IV ceftriaxone 2 g BD and vancomycin

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of progressive left calf swelling and pain. She returned from a 14-hour flight one week ago. She has no significant medical history, takes no regular medications, and has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism. Her renal function is normal. A compression ultrasound confirms an acute occlusive deep vein thrombosis of the left popliteal vein.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 128/76 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA, Temp 36.9
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal; UEC: eGFR >90 mL/min; LFTs normal; INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation regimen?

options.text: Warfarin with an INR target of 2.0 to 3.0 long-term
Enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg daily SC for 5 days then warfarin ongoing
Aspirin 100 mg daily for three months as sole antithrombotic
Rivaroxaban 15 mg BD for 21 days then 20 mg daily for 3 months
Dabigatran 150 mg BD following 5 days of parenteral enoxaparin

stem: A 52-year-old man is reviewed in the outpatient clinic 3 months after a segmental pulmonary embolism. It was unprovoked, with no transient risk factor identified, and age-appropriate cancer screening was negative. He has taken rivaroxaban 20 mg daily for 3 months without missed doses or bleeding, has no history of bleeding and takes no other medicines. He asks when he can stop anticoagulation.

data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-180); eGFR 92 mL/min/1.73 m2 (>60); liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Continue rivaroxaban with no planned stop date and regular review
Stop rivaroxaban now, as the 3-month treatment course is complete
Stop rivaroxaban and start aspirin 100 mg daily for extended prevention
Stop rivaroxaban and repeat a D-dimer in 4 weeks to guide restarting
Continue rivaroxaban 20 mg daily to 6 months in total, then stop

stem: A 22-year-old tall, thin man presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset right-sided pleuritic chest pain and mild dyspnoea that began 3 hours ago while at rest. He is a non-smoker with no significant medical history. He is not distressed and is speaking in full sentences. A chest X-ray confirms a moderate right-sided pneumothorax with a visible lung edge approximately 3 cm from the chest wall at the hilum.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 122/78 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 97% RA, Temp 36.8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Observe for 4 hours and repeat chest X-ray before discharge
Perform needle aspiration of the right hemithorax and reassess
Insert a large-bore intercostal drain connected to underwater seal
Arrange urgent cardiothoracic surgical review for thoracoscopy
Administer high-flow oxygen at 15 L/min via non-rebreather mask

stem: A 65-year-old man with a history of congestive heart failure and type 2 diabetes presents with progressive dyspnoea over 2 weeks. He has right-sided reduced breath sounds with dullness to percussion. A chest X-ray confirms a large right-sided pleural effusion. A diagnostic thoracentesis is performed.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 135/82 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 93% RA, Temp 36.9
data_table.Investigations: Serum: protein 62 g/L, LDH 180 U/L; Pleural fluid: protein 22 g/L, LDH 85 U/L, pH 7.42, glucose 5.8 mmol/L, cell count shows predominantly lymphocytes, no organisms on Gram stain

lead_in: How should this effusion be classified using Light's criteria?

options.text: Exudative, as the protein ratio exceeds the 0.5 threshold
Exudative, as the LDH ratio exceeds the 0.6 threshold value
Transudative, as none of the three Light's criteria are met
Exudative, because the glucose level is below serum glucose
Indeterminate, requiring pleural biopsy for definitive typing

stem: A 55-year-old man is referred to the sleep clinic by his GP for assessment of excessive daytime sleepiness and witnessed apnoeas. His wife reports loud snoring with episodes of gasping and choking during sleep. He has a BMI of 34, neck circumference of 44 cm, and a Mallampati score of IV. He has resistant hypertension requiring three antihypertensive medications. His Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 16 out of 24.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 148/94 mmHg (on three antihypertensives), HR 82
data_table.Examination: Crowded oropharynx, large tongue, retrognathia, neck circumference 44 cm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Overnight pulse oximetry at home as a screening assessment
Lateral cephalometric X-ray to assess upper airway anatomy
CT neck to exclude structural upper airway obstruction first
Arterial blood gas to assess for chronic respiratory failure
Polysomnography to confirm diagnosis and determine severity

subtopic_detail: Painful Horner syndrome after neck strain
stem: A 44-year-old man has three days of constant left periorbital and neck pain that began during a gym session. He has never had headaches before. There is no visual loss and he lies still with the pain.

data_table.Examination: Left ptosis and miosis, pupils reactive, no lacrimation; power and speech normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: CT angiography of the head and neck arteries today
High-flow oxygen by non-rebreather mask for the pain
Non-contrast CT brain and discharge if it is normal
Verapamil 80 mg three times daily and neurology review
Sumatriptan 6 mg subcutaneously and review in one week

stem: A 32-year-old woman of African descent presents with a 6-week history of dry cough, fatigue, and bilateral ankle swelling. She also reports painful raised red lesions on her shins. A chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with pulmonary infiltrates. Serum ACE level is elevated. A biopsy of a skin lesion shows non-caseating granulomas. Spirometry shows a mild restrictive pattern with an FVC of 72% predicted.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 96% RA, Temp 37.0
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal; UEC: eGFR >90, calcium 2.78 mmol/L (ref 2.15-2.55); ACE 98 U/L (ref 8-52); 24-hour urine calcium elevated; LFTs: ALP 145 U/L; spirometry: FVC 72%, FEV1 70%, FEV1/FVC 0.82; DLCO 65% predicted

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Observation only as sarcoidosis is usually self-limiting
Commence oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/day for 4 to 6 weeks
Start methotrexate 15 mg weekly as a steroid-sparing first line
Prescribe inhaled budesonide 800 mcg BD for pulmonary disease
Commence hydroxychloroquine 200 mg BD for skin and joint disease

stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a 12-month history of progressive exertional dyspnoea and a dry cough. He is a retired builder with 20 years of asbestos exposure. He has never smoked. Examination reveals bilateral fine inspiratory crackles at the lung bases and finger clubbing. High-resolution CT shows bilateral basal-predominant honeycombing with traction bronchiectasis and minimal ground glass opacity. Autoimmune serology is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 128/76 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 92% RA at rest
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry: FVC 58% predicted, FEV1 62% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.86; DLCO 38% predicted; HRCT: bilateral basal honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis, minimal GGO, subpleural distribution

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological management?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day tapering over three to six months
Azathioprine 2 mg/kg/day as immunosuppressive maintenance therapy
Commence pirfenidone or nintedanib as an antifibrotic agent
Commence sildenafil for secondary pulmonary hypertension
Prescribe N-acetylcysteine 600 mg TDS as an antioxidant therapy

stem: A 38-year-old woman presents to her GP with migraine headaches occurring 10 days per month for the past 6 months, significantly impacting her work. She uses sumatriptan for acute attacks, which provides relief but she is using it 3 to 4 times per week. She has a history of well-controlled asthma on a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid. Her BMI is 22 and blood pressure is normal. She is planning pregnancy in the next 12 months.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 114/68 mmHg, HR 72
data_table.Medications: Sumatriptan 50 mg PRN (3-4 times weekly), fluticasone 100 mcg BD inhaled

lead_in: What is the most appropriate prophylactic medication?

options.text: Propranolol 40 mg BD titrated up to effect over four weeks
Topiramate 25 mg daily titrated up to 50 to 100 mg daily
Sodium valproate 200 mg BD titrated up to effect over weeks
Amitriptyline 10 mg nocte titrated up to 25 to 50 mg nocte
Commence monthly galcanezumab CGRP monoclonal antibody injection

subtopic_detail: Large vessel occlusion stroke - thrombectomy eligibility
stem: A 72-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation (not on anticoagulation) presents to a regional emergency department 2 hours after sudden onset of right-sided hemiplegia, global aphasia, and forced left gaze deviation. Her NIHSS score is 18. A non-contrast CT brain shows no haemorrhage. CT angiography demonstrates a left middle cerebral artery M1 segment occlusion. CT perfusion shows a small core infarct volume (15 mL) with a large penumbra (120 mL mismatch). The nearest comprehensive stroke centre with endovascular capability is 90 minutes away by road.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88 (irregular), BP 172/94 mmHg, SpO2 96% RA, Temp 36.9, GCS 10
data_table.Investigations: BSL 8.2 mmol/L; INR 1.0; non-contrast CT: no haemorrhage, early subtle hypodensity left insula; CTA: left MCA M1 occlusion; CTP: core 15 mL, penumbra 120 mL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management strategy?

options.text: Administer IV alteplase and arrange retrieval for thrombectomy
Administer antiplatelet therapy and manage conservatively locally
Administer IV heparin infusion and arrange cardiology review
Reduce BP to <140/90 first, then consider thrombolysis and transfer
Give IV tenecteplase and arrange urgent transfer for thrombectomy

stem: A 66-year-old man received IV tenecteplase 45 minutes ago for an acute left MCA territory ischaemic stroke with an NIHSS of 12. He is not a candidate for thrombectomy. He has been admitted to the stroke unit. His neurological status is stable with no signs of haemorrhagic transformation. His BP has been fluctuating between 165-180/90-100 mmHg since admission.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78 (regular), BP 178/96 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 97% RA, Temp 37.0, GCS 12
data_table.Investigations: Repeat non-contrast CT at 24 hours: no haemorrhagic transformation

lead_in: What is the appropriate blood pressure target for the next 24 hours?

options.text: Maintain BP below 180/105 mmHg with IV antihypertensive PRN
Reduce BP to below 140/90 mmHg immediately with IV infusion
Allow permissive hypertension up to 220/120 mmHg post-thrombolysis
Target systolic BP of 120 to 130 mmHg with glyceryl trinitrate patch
Withhold all antihypertensives and monitor without intervention

stem: A 62-year-old woman with recently diagnosed metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma on gemcitabine-based chemotherapy develops acute left leg swelling. Compression ultrasound confirms an extensive iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis. She has normal renal function and no thrombocytopenia. She has no history of gastrointestinal bleeding. Her oncologist confirms she will continue chemotherapy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 97% RA
data_table.Investigations: FBC: Hb 108 g/L, WCC 5.2 x10^9/L, platelets 185 x10^9/L; UEC: eGFR >90; LFTs: mild cholestasis; coags: INR 1.1

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation strategy?

options.text: Warfarin with a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0 with LMWH bridging
Apixaban 10 mg BD for 7 days then 5 mg BD for at least 6 months
Subcutaneous enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg daily as the preferred option
Rivaroxaban 15 mg BD for 21 days then 20 mg daily for six months
Insert an IVC filter and defer anticoagulation due to cancer risk

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with a 4-day history of productive cough with rust-coloured sputum, fevers, and pleuritic chest pain. He has no significant comorbidities and takes no regular medications. He is alert and oriented. A chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation. He has no drug allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 98, BP 128/78 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 94% RA, Temp 38.8
data_table.Investigations: FBC: WCC 16.2 x10^9/L; CRP 185 mg/L; UEC: urea 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 85 micromol/L; albumin 34 g/L; ABG on RA: pH 7.42, pO2 68 mmHg, pCO2 36 mmHg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 1 g TDS for 5 days as outpatient treatment
IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily and oral azithromycin 500 mg daily
Oral amoxicillin 1 g TDS and oral doxycycline 100 mg BD for 5 days
IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g TDS for broad Gram-negative cover
Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 7 days as fluoroquinolone cover

stem: A 62-year-old man with severe COPD (FEV1 35% predicted) on home oxygen presents with sudden worsening of his baseline dyspnoea and right-sided pleuritic chest pain over the past 2 hours. He has a 45-pack-year smoking history and is on maximal inhaled therapy. On examination, breath sounds are markedly reduced on the right with hyperresonance to percussion. His chest X-ray confirms a moderate right-sided pneumothorax with no mediastinal shift.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 85% on 2 L/min nasal prong oxygen (baseline SpO2 91% on 2 L), Temp 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Chest X-ray: moderate right pneumothorax, bilateral emphysematous changes, no tension

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Attempt needle aspiration as first-line as per primary pneumothorax
Observe with supplemental oxygen and repeat imaging in 6 hours
Increase supplemental oxygen to 15 L/min via non-rebreather mask
Arrange urgent CT thorax before any intervention to plan approach
Insert a small-bore intercostal catheter connected to underwater seal

subtopic_detail: Offering an HIV test prompted by an indicator condition
stem: A 32-year-old man attends for review of shingles across two adjacent left thoracic dermatomes, treated with valaciclovir a week ago. He takes no regular medicines, has no diabetes, and has had several new sexual partners this year.

data_table.Examination: Crusting vesicular rash; no oral thrush, lymphadenopathy or weight loss
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and electrolytes normal; fasting glucose 4.9 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Offer HIV testing today after obtaining his consent
Start amitriptyline now to prevent postherpetic neuralgia
Measure serum immunoglobulins and lymphocyte subsets today
Arrange a computed tomography scan looking for malignancy
Give the recombinant zoster vaccine at this visit

stem: A 35-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with HIV after presenting with oral candidiasis and weight loss. Her initial workup is completed and ART is being commenced.

data_table.Investigations: CD4 count 85 cells/microL, HIV viral load 180,000 copies/mL. Toxoplasma IgG positive. CMV IgG positive. TB QuantiFERON negative. HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive.

lead_in: Which opportunistic infection prophylaxis regimen should be commenced alongside ART?

options.text: TMP-SMX for PJP plus valganciclovir for CMV prophylaxis given positive CMV serology and severe immunosuppression
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole plus azithromycin 1200 mg weekly for MAC prophylaxis at this stage
No prophylaxis required as ART initiation alone will restore CD4 count and prevent opportunistic infections
Dapsone 100 mg daily as first-line PJP prophylaxis plus pyrimethamine for toxoplasmosis cover
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg daily for both PJP and toxoplasmosis prophylaxis

stem: A 40-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV (CD4 45, VL 320,000) was commenced on ART and TMP-SMX prophylaxis 3 weeks ago. He also had latent TB treated with isoniazid commenced 2 weeks before ART. He now presents with worsening fevers, new cervical lymphadenopathy with fluctuance, and a new right middle lobe consolidation on chest X-ray. His CD4 has risen to 120 and viral load has dropped to 2,500.

data_table.Investigations: CD4 120 (was 45), VL 2,500 (was 320,000). CRP 142. CXR: RML consolidation.
data_table.Examination: Right cervical lymphadenopathy, fluctuant, tender. New cough.

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: ART treatment failure with progression of AIDS-defining tuberculosis at this stage
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome unmasking subclinical TB despite isoniazid prophylaxis
Community-acquired pneumonia unrelated to HIV as his improving immune status reduces infection susceptibility
Isoniazid-resistant TB that has broken through prophylaxis requiring second-line treatment
Drug reaction to ART presenting as a systemic inflammatory response at this stage

stem: A 25-year-old man who has sex with men presents requesting HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). He reports inconsistent condom use with casual partners and a recent diagnosis of rectal gonorrhoea treated 6 weeks ago. His 4th-generation HIV Ag/Ab test today is negative. He has a hepatitis B surface antigen positive result with HBeAg positive and HBV DNA of 28,000 IU/mL. His renal function shows eGFR 92.

data_table.Investigations: HIV 4th-gen Ag/Ab: negative. HBsAg positive, HBeAg positive, HBV DNA 28,000 IU/mL. eGFR 92. STI screen: pharyngeal and rectal GC/CT negative.
data_table.History: MSM. Inconsistent condoms. Recent rectal gonorrhoea.

lead_in: What critical consideration must be addressed before commencing tenofovir-emtricitabine PrEP?

options.text: The recent gonorrhoea diagnosis requires a repeat STI screen to confirm clearance before PrEP can start
Active hepatitis B is an absolute contraindication to tenofovir-emtricitabine PrEP and he should use condoms only
His eGFR of 92 is below the threshold for safe tenofovir use requiring renal referral before commencing
His chronic hepatitis B requires gastroenterology review as tenofovir cessation could trigger a severe HBV flare
On-demand (event-driven) PrEP rather than daily dosing should be prescribed to reduce cumulative tenofovir renal toxicity

stem: A 42-year-old man with untreated HIV (diagnosed today, CD4 32, VL 450,000) presents with 2 weeks of progressive headache, confusion, and low-grade fevers. He has no focal neurological signs. CT brain shows no mass lesion or hydrocephalus. Lumbar puncture opening pressure is 32 cmH2O.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8, HR 86, BP 128/78 mmHg, GCS 14 (E4V4M6)
data_table.Investigations: CSF: protein 0.62 g/L, glucose 2.1 mmol/L (serum 5.8), WCC 12 (predominantly lymphocytes). India ink preparation shows encapsulated yeast. Cryptococcal antigen titre CSF 1:2048.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Voriconazole as it has superior CNS penetration compared to amphotericin B for fungal meningitis and review clinical response at follow-up
High-dose fluconazole 1200 mg daily as induction therapy with mannitol for raised intracranial pressure with appropriate dose adjustment
Amphotericin B and flucytosine induction with immediate ART initiation to accelerate immune recovery and ongoing monitoring of progress
Liposomal amphotericin B with dexamethasone to reduce meningeal inflammation and intracranial pressure and review clinical response accordingly
IV amphotericin B deoxycholate plus flucytosine for at least 2 weeks induction, with daily therapeutic lumbar punctures to manage raised intracranial pressure

stem: A 30-year-old man from Myanmar who arrived in Australia 6 months ago as a refugee presents for routine health assessment. He is asymptomatic with no cough, fevers, or weight loss. He received BCG vaccination as an infant. His chest X-ray is normal. His QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus test returns positive.

data_table.Investigations: QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus: positive. CXR: normal. FBC normal. LFTs normal.
data_table.History: Myanmar-born, BCG vaccinated. Asymptomatic. Arrived Australia 6 months ago.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Treat latent TB with isoniazid 300 mg daily for 9 months with pyridoxine supplementation
No treatment needed as a positive QuantiFERON in a BCG-vaccinated individual is likely a false positive
Commence full 4-drug RIPE therapy as positive QuantiFERON with recent migration suggests active TB
Obtain three early-morning sputum samples for AFB smear and culture before any treatment decision
Observe without treatment and repeat QuantiFERON in 12 months as LTBI reactivation risk is low in young adults

stem: A 55-year-old man born in India presents with 6 weeks of productive cough, 5 kg weight loss, drenching night sweats, and low-grade fevers. He migrated to Australia 20 years ago. He is a taxi driver. Chest X-ray shows right upper lobe cavitating consolidation.

data_table.Investigations: CXR: right upper lobe cavitating consolidation with air-fluid level. Sputum AFB smear: positive (2+). HIV test: negative.
data_table.History: Born India. Productive cough 6 weeks, weight loss, night sweats.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action alongside commencing anti-TB treatment?

options.text: Wait for culture confirmation before notifying public health as AFB smear alone cannot confirm M. tuberculosis
Commence treatment and arrange outpatient follow-up as he is clinically stable and can self-isolate at home
Notify the state public health unit, isolate the patient in a negative-pressure room, and initiate contact tracing
Start treatment but defer contact tracing until drug susceptibility results are available to inform screening approach
Commence treatment and notify his GP as the reporting authority for communicable diseases

stem: A 60-year-old woman commenced on standard RIPE therapy (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for pulmonary TB presents at week 3 with nausea, vomiting, and right upper quadrant discomfort. She was well before treatment. She drinks no alcohol.

data_table.Investigations: ALT 380 U/L (baseline 22), AST 310 U/L (baseline 18), ALP 95 U/L, bilirubin 48 micromol/L, INR 1.1. HBsAg negative, HCV Ab negative.
data_table.Medications: Rifampicin 600 mg, isoniazid 300 mg, pyrazinamide 1500 mg, ethambutol 800 mg (all daily). Pyridoxine 25 mg daily.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reduce doses of all four drugs by 50% and monitor LFTs weekly while continuing treatment with appropriate dose adjustment
Cease all hepatotoxic agents (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide), continue ethambutol, and reintroduce sequentially once LFTs normalise
Cease pyrazinamide only as it is the most hepatotoxic agent and continue the other three drugs at this stage
Continue all drugs as transient transaminase elevation is expected and self-limiting in the first month
Switch to a fluoroquinolone-based regimen (moxifloxacin, ethambutol, injectable aminoglycoside) permanently

stem: A 38-year-old man born in Papua New Guinea presents with smear-positive pulmonary TB. He was treated for TB in PNG 3 years ago but reports completing only 3 months of a 6-month course due to medication access issues. GeneXpert MTB/RIF performed on his sputum detects M. tuberculosis with rifampicin resistance.

data_table.Investigations: Sputum AFB smear positive (3+). GeneXpert MTB/RIF: M. tuberculosis detected, rifampicin resistance detected. HIV negative.
data_table.History: Born PNG. Previous incomplete TB treatment (3 of 6 months). Current presentation: cough 8 weeks, haemoptysis, weight loss 8 kg.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start RIPE plus moxifloxacin as a five-drug intensive regimen while awaiting full DST results
Commence standard RIPE therapy as GeneXpert rifampicin resistance may be a false positive at this stage
Commence an MDR-TB regimen under specialist guidance and refer to the state TB service for ongoing management with DOT
Wait for full phenotypic drug susceptibility testing before commencing any treatment to tailor the regimen
Re-treat with the same RIPE regimen for a full 6-month course as the previous failure was due to non-adherence not resistance

stem: A 32-year-old woman from Zimbabwe is diagnosed with both smear-positive pulmonary TB and HIV (CD4 38, VL 520,000). She has commenced standard RIPE therapy. The clinical team is deciding when to start ART. She has no signs of cryptococcal disease and her serum CrAg screen is negative.

data_table.Investigations: CD4 38 cells/microL, VL 520,000. CrAg screen negative. Sputum AFB smear positive. TB drug susceptibility: pending.

lead_in: What is the optimal timing for ART initiation in this patient?

options.text: Within 2 weeks of commencing TB treatment given her profoundly low CD4 count at this stage
After completing the 2-month intensive phase of TB treatment to reduce drug interaction complexity
